22-
23-- The Trade-offs of Layered Architecture
24-
25:- Why Common Modeling Approaches Struggle at DAB- Star Schema at DAB
26-
27-- 3NF at DAB
28-
29-- Ensemble Modeling- Three Building Blocks
30-
31-- Why This Solves the Challenges
32-
33-- A Worked Example
34-
35-- The Trade-offs
36-
37-- Data according to Requirements (DAR)- Design Principles for DAR
38-
39-- Trade-offs in DAR
40-
41-- Conformity and the Limits of Discipline
42-
43-- What the Architecture Achieves Together
44-
45-When we set out to build an analytical data storage system, we face a problem that does not exist in operational software development. An operational system supports specific business processes with well-defined use cases that rarely change. Its design can be optimized for those interactions.
46-
47-Analytical systems are fundamentally different. Their purpose is to store data that supports analytical data products - reports, dashboards, models, explorations - most of which do not exist yet when the system is built. We are building for unknown requirements.
48-
49-This matters because humans gather knowledge sequentially. An answered question expands understanding, which surfaces new questions we could not have anticipated. A data product that starts simple can quickly become complex, and the system must accommodate this growth without breaking.
50-
--
150-
151-The DAB layer is the focal point of change in the architecture. As the system grows, new context and data are continuously added. We need a modeling approach that supports this growth without becoming rigid or driving complexity.
152-
153:### Star Schema at DAB
154-
155:Star Schema modeling rose in popularity in the late 1990s and remains widely used. It works well for specific data products in DAR, where its query-friendly structure is a genuine advantage. But it is not optimal for DAB, and the reason comes down to how it handles change.
156-
157:Star Schema builds broad tables - dimensions with many columns. Any broad table creates problems in a layer that serves as the source for all downstream data products.
158-
159-Consider adding a new attribute to a dimension in DAB for one specific data product. Multiple other data products use that same dimension but are not interested in the new attribute. Because we changed the loading code, we need to regression test all data products to verify we have not introduced side effects. We have built a dependency on structure and transformation logic that should not exist.
160-
161-The broader the table, the more complex the transformation code. When loading thirty attributes into one table, the transformation logic for each often has its own joins and conditions. Left Joins and Full Outer Joins accumulate - certain joins only applicable to some attributes, but all required to produce the single broad table. Over time, these pipelines become so complex that nobody wants to touch them. Time to market degrades until the system becomes unmanageable.
162-
163-### 3NF at DAB
164-
165:Third Normal Form is sometimes considered for DAB. While 3NF provides better normalization than Star Schema, it shares a similar challenge: the hierarchical nature of 3NF, where foreign keys cascade through table structures, means that changing the granularity of a relationship can cascade through larger areas of the data model. The rework becomes significant - not only in table definitions but in rewriting transformation code, reloading data, and rewriting all DAR data products to match the changed DAB model.
166-
167-What we need is non-destructive change: the ability to add new structures and code without modifying what already exists.
168-
169-## Ensemble Modeling
170-
171-In the late 1990s and early 2000s, several practitioners independently recognized that conventional modeling techniques were not suited to how analytical systems actually change. Three approaches emerged:
172-
173-- `Data Vault` by Dan Linstedt
174-
175-- `Focal Framework` by Per Olof Eriksson
176-
177-- `Anchor Modeling` by Olle Regardt and Lars Ronnback
178-
179-These share enough in their fundamental approach that Hans Hultgren grouped them under the term Ensemble Modeling in 2014. They all solve the same problem: how to handle continuous change in a modular, non-destructive way.
180-
181-### Three Building Blocks
182-
183-Ensemble Modeling decomposes the data model into three types of objects, each directly addressing the challenges described earlier:
184-
185-`Core Business Concept` - represents an entity and how it is identified. These objects contain only identification and are immutable. They hold no history, no descriptive data, and never need to change once created - the most fundamental representation of an entity is separated from everything else, creating a stable focal point that subsequent additions build on without modifying.
186-
187:`Description` - holds descriptive data about a Core Business Concept. Each Description has a direct relationship to one Core Business Concept and maintains its own history. Crucially, each Description is independent: adding a new one does not touch existing Descriptions or their loading pipelines. In contrast with Star Schema, where adding a new attribute means modifying the existing dimension and its loading logic, Ensemble Modeling adds a new Description object alongside existing ones. The transformation code handles only that attribute - a single, focused pipeline.
188-
189-`Association` - holds relationships between Core Business Concepts. There are no foreign keys between Core Business Concept objects; relationships are always resolved through Associations. They handle all cardinality types and maintain their own history. Entities are structurally independent within the model, and relationships can be added or extended without touching the entities they connect.
190-
191-### Why This Solves the Challenges
192-
193-The independence between objects is what makes the approach work. We can model an entity fully without resolving any of its relationships to other entities, and add those relationships later through Associations - without modifying existing structure or code.
194-
195-Because structures and their associated pipelines are independent, we can load and catch up history without affecting other pipelines. We could implement a new entity, load it with three years of historical data, and later add an Association to an existing entity - all without touching the rest of the model.
196-
197-This is Micro Agility: the ability to handle small, continuous changes - new attributes, new entities, new relationships - in a modular way that never requires modifying existing structures or code. Combined with the Macro Agility from the layered architecture, the system handles both types of change throughout its life cycle.
198-
199-### A Worked Example
200-
201-Consider a single new requirement: the business wants to start recording each customer's preferred contact channel.
202-
203:In a Star Schema DAB, this is a new column on the Customer dimension. It requires an ALTER to a table already in use, a change to the loading job that populates it, and a decision about the history that predates the new column - three modifications to structure and code that other data products already depend on, followed by regression testing to confirm nothing downstream broke.
204-
205-In Ensemble Modeling, it is one new Description object attached to the Customer Core Business Concept, with its own focused pipeline. Nothing that already exists is touched. The other data products do not see the addition, because their structures and loading logic are unchanged. There is no regression surface, because there was no modification.
206-
207:The difference is not the effort of this one change. It is that the Star Schema approach has coupled the new attribute to everything that shares the dimension, while Ensemble Modeling has kept it isolated. Repeated across the thousands of such changes a platform absorbs over its life cycle, that difference is what separates a system that stays maintainable from one that does not.
208-
209:One caveat is worth stating precisely, because the three approaches are often treated as interchangeable on this point and they are not. The additive path - expressing every change as a new structure - is guaranteed to different degrees. Anchor Modeling and the Focal Framework are strict by construction: a new attribute is necessarily a new structure, because there is no broad table to alter. Data Vault is the looser case. Because it groups descriptive attributes into satellites, the same new attribute can be added either as a new satellite, which is additive, or as a column on an existing satellite, which is a modification - the Star Schema problem reappearing inside the supposedly additive layer. Data Vault permits the additive path but does not compel it; whether the model stays additive is left to the modeler rather than guaranteed by the technique.
210-
211-### The Trade-offs
212-
213:Ensemble Modeling introduces its own costs. The granular structure means significantly more tables than Star Schema or 3NF. Querying DAB directly requires joining across many objects, making it less convenient for ad-hoc exploration (though this is what DAR is for). There is a learning curve: the approach is less intuitive for practitioners accustomed to broad tables, and tooling support varies. Teams should expect an investment in training before the benefits fully materialize. Many automation tools have emerged to address this, and declarative approaches are making it even easier to build with these techniques.
214-
215-The trade-off is structural simplicity of individual pipelines against a larger number of objects. In practice, the simplicity of each pipeline makes the overall system more maintainable than fewer but more complex pipelines, especially as the system grows.
216-
217-## Data according to Requirements (DAR)
218-
219-DAR is where we build data products from the integrated data in DAB. There is no prescribed modeling technique or semantic rule. The goal is to deliver direct business value and make data as accessible as possible.
220-
221:Star Schema, Activity Schema, One Big Table - whatever suits the analytical need and visualization tooling. This is where Star Schema belongs: its query-friendly structure and intuitive design are genuine strengths for making data accessible to business users and BI tools. The broad tables that are problematic in DAB are perfectly appropriate in DAR, where each data product controls its own structures.
222-
223-### Design Principles for DAR
224-
225-A few rules govern this layer:
226-
227-`Data comes from DAB.` All data products in DAR source from the business layer. This preserves the dependency-breaking architecture - if a DAR product reaches back to DAS or a source system, the cascade-of-change protection is bypassed.
228-
229-`No cross-dependencies between data products.` Each data product owns its physical structures, and those structures are not reused by other data products. You can have five Customer dimensions in DAR - one for each data product. While this may seem counterproductive, the reasoning is the same cascade-of-change logic: if one data product wants to add context to its Customer dimension, it should not affect the others. Each data product has its own life cycle and rate of change - coupling them reintroduces the dependency problem at the consumption layer.
230-
231-This runs against the instinct to build conformed dimensions - a single shared Customer dimension that every data product consumes, precisely so that they agree. That instinct is right about the goal and wrong about the mechanism. Consistency does not require a shared physical structure; it requires a shared definition. In this architecture the definition lives in DAB, where Customer is integrated and resolved exactly once. Every per-product Customer dimension in DAR is built from that single definition, so the five dimensions agree on the facts because they descend from the same source of meaning, not because they are the same table. The rule, stated compactly: reuse the definition, never reuse the instance. The conformed dimension buys consistency by sharing structure and pays for it in coupling; with a real integration layer beneath it, that price is unnecessary, because consistency has already been secured upstream where meaning is defined.
232-
233-`Optimize for the consumer.` DAR is the place to denormalize, aggregate, pre-calculate - whatever makes the data product effective for its users. The integration complexity has been handled in DAB; DAR focuses purely on serving the requirement.
234-
235-### Trade-offs in DAR
236-
237-The no-cross-dependency rule means some transformation logic is duplicated across data products. This is a conscious trade-off: we accept some duplication to maintain independence. We can accept this because building an analytical table in DAR is straightforward - all integration logic has been handled in DAB. The alternative - shared structures that create dependencies - reintroduces the very problem the architecture solves.
238-
239-There is also an organizational dimension. When data products are independent, teams can own and evolve them without coordination overhead. When they share structures, every change requires cross-team negotiation - a bottleneck that slows delivery and frustrates everyone involved.
240-
241-## Conformity and the Limits of Discipline
242-
243-There is a prior condition underneath everything described so far, and it is where most implementations actually fail. A layered architecture only breaks dependencies if every consumer genuinely routes through DAB instead of reaching past it to a convenient source. An additive model only stays additive if every engineer expresses the next change as a new structure rather than quietly editing an existing one. The architecture names the conforming move; it does not, by itself, perform it.
244-
245-What keeps a system maintainable is conformity - the same patterns, the same boundaries, the same rules applied the same way every time. A platform whose conventions are followed consistently stays simple enough to reason about; one riddled with one-off exceptions does not, regardless of how sound its architecture looked on the diagram. The gradual loss of maintainability that every long-lived platform risks is, described precisely, what an accumulation of non-conforming exceptions looks like over time.
246-

Published onThursday, January 22, 2026

# The Anatomy of a Business Question

Authors- NameSiavoush MohammadiTwitter

## The Coffee Machine Test

Consider this exchange at the coffee machine:

`"How were sales last quarter?"

"Good! We increased it by 10%"

Both parties walk away satisfied. The conversation worked. But what actually happened? Did sales increase 10% across all customer segments? All product groups? Are we talking about orders placed or orders delivered? Gross or net of returns?

None of those questions came up because they didn't need to. Both people share context - years of it. They know which products matter, which metrics the company tracks, what "good" means. The ambiguity wasn't a bug; it was efficient communication between people who share tribal knowledge.

Now try building a dashboard from that question.

## The Interface Mismatch

The difficulty people have formulating business questions isn't about intelligence or capability. It's about an interface mismatch.

Human communication evolved for context-rich environments. We're remarkably good at filling in gaps, inferring meaning, and navigating ambiguity. When you ask a colleague about sales, you're not just exchanging words - you're drawing on shared meetings, past conversations, company history, and implicit understanding of what matters.

Data systems have none of this. A dashboard doesn't know that "customer" means something different in marketing than in finance. A KPI definition can't intuit that "active" should probably exclude test accounts. A data model doesn't remember that conversation you had about seasonal adjustments.

This creates a genuine translation problem. People aren't asking bad questions - they're asking questions designed for human listeners, then expecting data systems to understand them.

## What Makes a Question Answerable?

Questions that data systems can actually answer have a predictable structure:

`"What is the [AGGREGATION] of [MEASURE] per [DIMENSION], [DIMENSION]?"

For example:

- "How many unique accounts have completed at least one purchase in the last 90 days, per week and acquisition channel?"

This sounds clunky compared to "How are customers doing?" But notice what the clunky version gives you:

- `The measure` is defined: unique accounts with completed purchase

- `The time window` is explicit: last 90 days

- `The dimensions` are stated: week and acquisition channel

- `The aggregation` is clear: a count

You could build a query from this. You could build a dashboard. You know exactly what "customer" means in this context because it's defined right in the question.

## The Evolution of a Question

What's interesting is watching a question transform as the ambiguity gets squeezed out:

`Stage 0` - The demand: "I need customer numbers!"

This isn't even a question. It's a statement that could mean almost anything.

`Stage 1` - The vague question: "How many customers do we have?"

Better - it's a question now. But customers who have ever purchased? Currently active? In trial? As of when?

`Stage 2` - The precise question: "How many unique accounts have completed at least one purchase in the last 90 days, per week and acquisition channel?"

Now we know what we're measuring, how we're slicing it, and what time period we care about.

`Stage 3` - The question with definitions: The precise question, plus explicit definitions for every term that could be ambiguous. What exactly counts as "completed"? What are the valid acquisition channels? Is week ISO week or something else?

The gap between Stage 0 and Stage 3 isn't trivial. It requires real thinking about what you actually want to know and why.

## Why This Matters Beyond Data

This same problem shows up in working with AI agents.

In designing for agentic experience, I called this "the sticky-note problem" - we pass AI fragments without context, expecting it to guess our standards and preferences. The underlying issue is the same: systems built for humans rely on shared context that never gets made explicit.

The qualities that make systems work well with AI agents - clear semantic definitions, explicit rules and boundaries, documented processes instead of tribal knowledge - these are exactly what makes business questions answerable by data systems.

In both cases, the solution isn't smarter technology. It's making the implicit explicit. Writing down what we actually mean. Defining our terms. Acknowledging that the receiver of our communication doesn't have access to everything in our heads.

There's another use case worth mentioning: validating data models. A well-formed question decomposes directly into model requirements - the measure reveals what entity you need, the dimensions reveal its attributes. If your data model can't answer the questions stakeholders actually ask, the model has gaps. The questions become a specification.

## Common Failure Modes

A few patterns worth watching for:

`The missing question mark.` "Monthly active users by region." This sounds complete, but it's actually a statement masquerading as a question. Force it into question form - "How many monthly active users do we have per region?" - and you'll naturally start asking what "active" means, which regions, and what defines a month.

`Undefined terms.` "How many churned customers per month?" Churned could mean canceled subscription, hasn't purchased in six months, explicitly requested deletion, or failed payment. The person asking probably has one of these in mind. The data system needs to know which one.

`The compound question.` "How many new and returning customers do we have per channel, and what's their average order value?" Two questions pretending to be one. They need different grains, different visualizations, different contexts. Split them.

`Missing time dimension.` "What's our conversion rate by landing page?" When? All time? Last month? Is this a snapshot or a trend? Every business question has a time dimension, even if it's not obvious.

## The Real Difficulty

The reason this is genuinely hard - not a matter of just trying harder - is that it requires a kind of context-switching that doesn't come naturally.

When you're thinking about your business, you're immersed in context. You know what matters, what's been discussed, what decisions are pending. Stepping outside that to ask "but what would someone with zero context need to know?" is cognitively expensive. It feels pedantic. It slows things down.

But the alternative is worse: meetings where 30 minutes are spent debating what "active user" means, three teams calculating the same metric three different ways, reports that contradict each other, dashboards nobody trusts.

The upfront work of defining terms and making questions precise isn't overhead - it's the actual work. Skip it, and you'll do it later, more expensively, when the dashboard is already built and the numbers don't match.

## A Practical Starting Point

If you're trying to improve how your organization asks business questions, here's where I'd start:

Pick one important question your team asks regularly. Go through the exercise of making it fully explicit: What's the measure? What are the dimensions? What's the time grain? Define every term that might be interpreted differently by different people.

It might feel tedious the first time. But once you've done it, you have something you can actually build from. And more importantly, you have a template for how questions should be asked.

The formula isn't magic. It's just a structure that forces the translation between how humans naturally communicate and what data systems need to hear.

At the coffee machine, ambiguity is fine. At the dashboard, it's expensive.

# Architecture decision records

One file per decision, numbered, in [MADR](https://adr.github.io/madr/) format. A record is
**superseded by a new file, never edited**, because the value of a decision record is the record
of what was true when it was made.

An ADR lands **before** the code it decides. A decision record written afterwards records what
was built, not what was decided.

| # | Decision | Slice |
|---|---|---|
| [0000](0000-use-madr.md) | Decisions are recorded as MADR files in this directory | 0 |
=== 0000 ===
---
status: accepted
date: 2026-09-07
decision-makers: [adss maintainers]
slice: 0
---

# Decisions are recorded as MADR files, written before the code they decide

## Context and Problem Statement

This system is built for a life cycle measured in decades, and almost every difficult thing about
it is a choice that had alternatives. Six months from now the question will not be "what does this
code do" — that is readable — but "what else was considered, and what did we know at the time".

Without a record, the answer is reconstructed from the code, which can only ever show the option
that won. The alternatives, the constraint that ruled them out, and the cost that was knowingly
accepted are all invisible, so the next person either re-litigates a settled question or, worse,
quietly reverses it without knowing there was a decision there at all.

## Decision Drivers

* the reasoning has to outlive the person who did it
* a reader must be able to tell a considered trade-off from an accident
* a record must be cheap enough to write that it actually gets written
* the record must be readable by an agent with no conversation history

## Considered Options

* MADR files in the repository, one per decision, written before the code
* MADR files written after the implementation, describing what was built
* Decisions recorded in pull request descriptions
* Decisions recorded in an external wiki
* No formal record; rely on commit messages

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: **MADR files under `docs/adr/`, numbered, written before the code they decide.**

Three properties make it the right one.

*In the repository.* The decision travels with the code it governs, is reviewed in the same pull
request, and is available to anyone — or anything — reading the repository with no other access.
An external wiki is a second surface that drifts from the code, and a pull request description is
unfindable six months later without knowing which pull request to open.

*Before the code.* This is the part that does real work. Writing the options out before building
forces the alternatives to be stated while they are still live, and it regularly changes the
answer — which is the whole return on the exercise. A record written afterwards can only describe
what was built, and its "considered options" section is reconstruction.

*Superseded, never edited.* Editing a record to match current reality destroys the thing that
made it worth keeping. A decision that has changed gets a new file that supersedes the old one, so
both the old reasoning and the reason it stopped holding survive.

The format is MADR because it names the parts that matter — context, drivers, options, outcome,
consequences — and because "Consequences" is where the honest cost goes. A record with only good
consequences has not been thought about.

### Consequences

* Good, because the reasoning behind every non-obvious choice is recoverable by anyone reading
  the repository, with no conversation history and no access to the people involved
* Good, because writing the alternatives down before building routinely changes what gets built
* Good, because a decision and the code implementing it are reviewed together
* Good, because [deviations.md](../deviations.md) has somewhere to point: the register is the
  index, the ADR is the argument
* Bad, because it is friction on every non-trivial change, and friction is what gets skipped under
  deadline pressure. The mitigation is that the bar is "a decision that had alternatives", not
  "every change" — a record for an obvious choice is noise that trains people to ignore the rest
* Bad, because a superseded record left in place can be read as current by someone who does not
  check the index or the `status` field

### Confirmation

The index in [README.md](README.md) lists every record. A pull request that changes an
architectural choice without an accompanying record is incomplete, and that is a review check
rather than an automated one — no linter can tell an architectural decision from a rename.

# The duckdb dialect is required, not preferred: postgres cannot parse QUALIFY.
[sqlfluff]
dialect = duckdb
templater = raw
max_line_length = 120

exclude_rules = AL09, RF06, LT05, LT09

=== README ===
# adss

An **Analytical Data Storage System**, built as [blog.daana.dev](https://blog.daana.dev)
describes one: three layers, one direction of flow, and no shortcuts between them.

| Layer | Schemas | What it does | Engine |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DAS** — data according to the *system* | `das__raw`, `das__staged` | captures the source as it arrived, persists it append-only, unpacks it strictly per contract | [dlt](https://dlthub.com) → hive-partitioned parquet → DuckDB views |
| **DAB** — data according to the *business* | `dab`, `dab__stage`, `dab__meta` | the integrated business model, and the only place the data is explained | `daana-cli` focal model |
| **DAR** — data according to the *requirements* | `dar__uss` | a **generated** Unified Star Schema: one event bridge, one peripheral per entity, one calendar | the ADSS USS generator |

Destinations read `dar__uss` and nothing else.

The layer names are not decoration. They are the principles — see
[docs/blueprint.md](docs/blueprint.md).

## Status

Slice 0: the scaffold. The layers, the questions that accept them, and the skills that describe
them arrive in the slices that follow.

## Getting started

```bash
uv sync --all-groups
uv run adss --version
uv run pytest
uv run pre-commit run --all-files
```

## Slices

Each slice answers one business question, and the presentation of that answer is what the slice
is accepted on. It is the prototype, not a report generated afterwards.

| # | Question | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many orders were placed per order month and ship country? | not started |

## Reading order

| Document | What it is |
|---|---|
| [docs/blueprint.md](docs/blueprint.md) | the principles, technology-free, no exceptions |
| [docs/conventions.md](docs/conventions.md) | the one convention document: naming, SQL, YAML, Python, commits |
| [docs/adr/](docs/adr/README.md) | one record per decision, written before the code it decides |
| [docs/deviations.md](docs/deviations.md) | every knowing departure from a principle, with its cost and its exit condition |
| [docs/questions/](docs/questions/) | the business questions, and the two queries that must agree on each answer |

HEADLINE: A dlt resource with `columns={"payload": {"data_type": "json"}}` lands each source record as exactly one JSON column with zero child tables and zero column inference — but dlt silently renames the dataset `das__raw` to `das_raw` unless you pass `enable_dataset_name_normalization=False`, and DuckDB silently drops columns across an evolving parquet glob unless you pass `union_by_name => true`.
--- 0 `uv add "dlt[filesystem,duckdb,parquet]" duckdb` works with no system-wide install and no .dlt config directory needed. dlt 1.30.0, duckdb 1.5.5, pyarrow 25.0.1.
--- 1 APPROACH B WINS: `@dlt.resource(columns={"payload": {"data_type": "json"}})` yielding a real dict under `payload` keeps the whole record in ONE column of dlt type `json`. No columns are inferred from inside it.
--- 2 Approach B survives NESTED objects and arrays with no child tables. A record containing {"Nested":{"a":1,"b":{"c":2}},"Arr":[{"x":1},{"x":2}]} produced no `probe_b_jsonhint__arr` table.
--- 3 APPROACH A also works: pre-serialising with json.dumps() gives a `text` column that DuckDB's JSON operators read identically. It is physically indistinguishable from B in parquet.
--- 4 APPROACH C FAILS the requirement: `max_table_nesting=0` does NOT stop normalisation. Top-level keys are still split into snake_cased typed columns; it only collapses NESTED values into json strings instead of child tables.
--- 5 120 real Northwind Orders records (2 pages x $top=60 with $skip) landed to local filesystem parquet. The API reports @odata.count=830 total.
--- 6 Default filesystem layout is <bucket_url>/<dataset>/<table>/<load_id>.<file_id>.parquet — one parquet file per table per load, plus an `init` marker and three _dlt_* bookkeeping folders.
--- 7 DESCRIBE of the landed parquet from DuckDB: payload is VARCHAR, dlt `timestamp` becomes TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, `bigint` becomes BIGINT.
--- 8 dlt adds EXACTLY TWO metadata columns to a root table: `_dlt_load_id` and `_dlt_id`. Nothing else. They are NOT sufficient for 'which load, from where, when'.
--- 9 `_dlt_load_id` is only a unix-timestamp-ish string; the load's completion time and schema name live in a SEPARATE `_dlt_loads/*.jsonl` file — written as JSONL even when loader_file_format='parquet'. It is joinable but requires read_json_auto.
--- 10 `_dlt_id` is a per-row-instance surrogate, NOT a stable record identity. The same source record (OrderId 10248) got a different _dlt_id in each load. Content identity must come from your own hash column.
--- 11 write_disposition='append' leaves earlier files intact. Two runs of the identical pipeline produced two parquet files per table and two rows in _dlt_loads; nothing was overwritten.
--- 12 CRITICAL: dataset_name='das__raw' is silently normalised to 'das_raw' (double underscore collapsed). Passing enable_dataset_name_normalization=False on the destination preserves the literal 'das__raw' folder.
--- 13 CRITICAL: a plain read_parquet glob over an append-only lake SILENTLY DROPS columns added in later loads — no error, just missing data. `union_by_name => true` fixes it.
--- 14 DuckDB JSON operators work directly on the VARCHAR payload column with an implicit cast — no explicit ::JSON needed. `->>` yields VARCHAR (then CAST), `->` yields JSON, plus json_keys / json_array_length / json_extract.
--- 15 The strict layer recovers precision the forgiving layer would have lost: freight is DOUBLE when dlt infers it (approach C), but DECIMAL(18,4) when cast explicitly out of the JSON column. This is a concrete argument for the two-layer design.
--- 16 Hive-style date partitioning works via the filesystem `layout` parameter, but the placeholder names are {YYYY}/{MM}/{DD}, not {year}/{month}/{day}.
--- 17 Your own provenance columns pass through untouched, including names with leading underscores and a non-normalised prefix like `das_`. Timestamps land as dlt `timestamp` -> parquet -> DuckDB TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE.

HEADLINE: marimo 0.24.0 reads DuckDB and renders title/prose/table/chart cleanly (altair, plotly and matplotlib ALL work with zero setup off a polars frame), and headless screenshots are solid — but `marimo export html` produces a NON-self-contained file that loads every frontend asset from cdn.jsdelivr.net and renders as a 100%-white blank page offline, so screenshots must come from the running server or from `marimo export thumbnail --execute`, never from the exported HTML.
--- 0 `uv add marimo duckdb` works instantly and marimo 0.24.0 is a lean install — 26 packages, NO pandas, NO numpy, NO plotting library. marimo uses narwhals as its dataframe-agnostic layer.
--- 1 `duckdb_result.pl()` (polars) silently needs pyarrow. Without it every downstream cell fails, and `marimo export html` exits with a clear error naming it. This is the first thing that will bite the DAR layer.
--- 2 All THREE plotting libraries render inside marimo with zero extra setup, each fed a polars DataFrame directly (pandas is not installed anywhere in this venv). Verified visually in a full-page screenshot: altair bar via mo.ui.altair_chart, plain altair line chart, plotly.express bar, and matplotlib A
--- 3 altair is the cleanest fit: it is the only one with a first-class marimo wrapper (`mo.ui.altair_chart`) giving selection/interaction, it takes polars natively, and its output is embedded as a vega spec in exports. plotly renders but grabs full container width and is visually heavy. matplotlib works 
--- 4 `marimo run` serves headless on a fixed port with no browser and no token. It comes up in ~1 second and serves fully LOCAL assets (./assets/...), so the running app works with no internet at all.
--- 5 CRITICAL: `marimo export html` output is NOT self-contained. Every JS/CSS/font is rewritten to https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@marimo-team/frontend@<version>/dist/... . Rendered offline it is a literally blank white page.
--- 6 The exported HTML DOES embed executed outputs (chart specs, table data, matplotlib raster) — the export runs the notebook itself, so no prior execution is needed. Size is 111,079 bytes for this 8-cell notebook. `--include-code` (default) and `--no-include-code` produce byte-identical SIZES but diffe
--- 7 Playwright 1.62.0 (python) does NOT match the pre-installed chromium in /opt/pw-browsers: it wants build 1234, only 1194 is present. Two independent fixes both proven to work.
--- 8 Screenshotting the RUNNING app works and produces a real render. Proven three ways: playwright's own DOM assertions, a PIL colour census, and reading the PNG back visually.
--- 9 marimo has a BUILT-IN headless screenshotter — `marimo export thumbnail` — which drives playwright internally. With `--execute` it starts nothing, needs no server, needs no CDN, and renders the full app including all charts. This is the best PR-acceptance mechanism found.
--- 10 `--execute` is mandatory for thumbnails. The DEFAULT is `--no-execute`, which renders notebook structure only and produces NO outputs — a thumbnail of an empty app.
--- 11 marimo creates a config file under XDG config on first run and needs that dir writable. It never once complained about the absence of a TTY — the entire spike ran with stdin and stdout both non-tty.
--- 12 `marimo export html` writes a session cache directory next to the notebook. This needs gitignoring in the real repo.
--- 13 Playwright's `full_page=True` gave exactly the viewport height, not the document height, on the marimo app — so a short viewport silently truncates the screenshot. Set a tall viewport instead. (No overflow:scroll container was detectable; document.scrollHeight simply equals the viewport.)
--- 14 Full marimo export format list for 0.24.0.
--- 15 marimo internally supports overriding the CDN asset base (`asset_url`, and `{version}` templating), but `marimo export html` exposes NO CLI flag for it — it is only reachable through the Python export API / server config.
--- 16 DuckDB DECIMAL leaks through to the frontend as polars `decimal[38,0]` and altair cannot encode it — I had to CAST(... AS DOUBLE) in SQL. The DAR views should cast aggregates to DOUBLE for the marimo layer.

GOTCHAS
- `marimo export html` output is NOT self-contained — it rewrites every JS/CSS/font to https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@marimo-team/frontend@<version>/dist/. Rendered without internet it is a 100%-white blank page (I measured exactly 1 distinct colour). Never screenshot the exported HTML for PR acceptanc
- pyarrow is a hidden hard requirement. `uv add marimo duckdb` gives you neither pyarrow nor pandas, and `duckdb.execute(...).pl()` then dies with `No module named 'pyarrow'` in every dependent cell. Add pyarrow explicitly.
- Playwright 1.62.0 looks for chromium build 1234; /opt/pw-browsers only has 1194. This breaks raw playwright AND marimo's own `export thumbnail` (which has no --executable-path flag). Fix with a symlink tree at a private PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH — do not run `playwright install`.
- `marimo export thumbnail` defaults to --no-execute, which renders notebook STRUCTURE ONLY and produces a thumbnail with no outputs. You must pass --execute.
- Playwright's full_page=True returns exactly the viewport height on a marimo app, not the document height — a 1000px viewport silently truncated the screenshot and lost two charts below the fold. Set a tall viewport (e.g. 1440x3400) rather than relying on full_page.
- Charts need a settle delay. `wait_until="networkidle"` is not enough: marimo streams cell outputs over a WebSocket after page load, and vega/plotly paint after that. Wait on a text selector from an actual cell output, then on `.vega-embed/.js-plotly-plot/img`, then an extra ~3s. marimo's own thumbna
- DuckDB DECIMAL columns arrive as polars `decimal[38,0]` and altair cannot encode them. CAST aggregates to DOUBLE in the SQL (this is a DAR-view design decision, not a notebook workaround).
- Anchor the DuckDB path on `pathlib.Path(__file__).parent`, not the cwd. `marimo export` / `export thumbnail` are often invoked from elsewhere and a relative path breaks silently.
- Open the warehouse with `duckdb.connect(path, read_only=True)`. DuckDB single-writer locking means a marimo app holding a read-write handle will block dlt or daana-cli from writing to the same file.
- marimo auto-creates /root/.config/marimo/marimo.toml (0 bytes) on first invocation — the XDG config dir must be writable. It made no complaint at all about the absence of a TTY (stdin and stdout both non-tty throughout this spike).
- `marimo export html` drops a `__marimo__/session/<notebook>.py.json` cache directory next to the notebook. Gitignore it.
- Export failure is visible but soft: cells that raise are printed as `MarimoExceptionRaisedError: ...` and the command ends with `Error: Export was successful, but some cells failed to execute.` — the HTML is still written. Check the exit code in CI; do not assume a produced file means a good file.

content.content:
HEADLINE: Every tool works and the whole gate goes green from a local venv with zero network: sqlfluff 4.3.0 has a real `duckdb` dialect that parses QUALIFY and quoted `"order"` cleanly, and `ty --error all` catches frozen-dataclass mutation, Literal-discriminator violations and union arg errors with no false positives — the only real fight is four sqlfluff rules (AL09, RF06, LT05, LT09) that structurally contradict how a code generator emits SQL and must be excluded, not fixed.
--- 0 sqlfluff 4.3.0 ships a first-class `duckdb` dialect, inheriting from postgres. No stand-in needed.
--- 1 The duckdb dialect is REQUIRED, not merely nicer: the same file under `postgres` fails to parse the QUALIFY clause entirely.
--- 2 On well-formatted generated SQL (UNION ALL of 3 branches, every column AS-aliased, cast(x AS DECIMAL(28,8)), lower-case functions, UPPER keywords, QUALIFY row_number() OVER (...), quoted reserved word `dab."order"`), the ONLY rule that fires under sqlfluff defaults is RF06. Running with `--rules all` produces an identi
--- 3 The quoted reserved word `dab."order"` is NOT flagged by RF06 — sqlfluff's duckdb dialect knows the quoting is necessary there. Only mixed-case identifiers are flagged.
--- 4 Realistic single-line generator output (no pretty-printing) fires 7 distinct rules. This is the real fight list.
--- 5 AL09 is the single most dangerous rule for this build. The brief's own requirement — 'each branch aliasing every column of one fixed column list with AS' — is exactly what AL09 forbids. It fired twice on `o.order_id AS order_id` and `o.order_status AS order_status`. It did NOT fire in file 1 only because every column t
--- 6 `sqlfluff fix` auto-repairs CV11 and LT14 but cannot repair RF02. Autofix rewrote `c.customer_name::VARCHAR` to `cast(c.customer_name AS VARCHAR)` and broke WHERE/GROUP onto their own lines.
--- 7 `ty` 0.0.78 IS viable. At DEFAULT severity it already catches all three deliberate errors in the frozen-dataclass / StrEnum / Literal-discriminated-union module: wrong argument type against a `A | B | C` union alias, assignment to a frozen dataclass field, and an out-of-Literal discriminator value.
--- 8 ty in STRICT mode (`--error all`) produces ZERO false positives on the good domain module — no friction from `@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)`, `StrEnum`, `tuple[Column, ...]`, `field(default_factory=tuple)`, the `A | B | C` union alias, or `match`/`case`/`assert_never` exhaustiveness.
--- 9 ty has no `strict = true` preset in 0.0.78 — strictness is the CLI flag `--error all` (or `--warn`/`--ignore` per rule, or `[tool.ty.rules]` severities in pyproject.toml). `ty check --help` lists `--error <RULE>` with 'Use "all" to apply to all rules'.
--- 10 ty --error all catches Any-leakage and bare generics that mypy --strict catches (`missing-type-argument`, `unsound-return-statement`), but does NOT flag a fully unannotated `def f(x, y)`. That gap must be closed by ruff's ANN rules, which do flag it.
--- 11 yamllint defaults fire exactly two rules on a data-contract YAML: `document-start` (missing `---`) as a warning, and `line-length` (80 default) as an error. The short flow mappings `{source_path: OrderId, target_name: order_id, type: INTEGER}` are accepted by the default `braces` rule with no complaint.
--- 12 pre-commit runs every hook from the local uv venv with `repo: local` + `language: system`. No remote repository is cloned — the pre-commit cache contains only its lock, README and db, no repo checkouts. CI determinism is therefore fully under uv.lock.
--- 13 The full gate goes green end to end on the six hooks.
--- 14 ruff 0.16.6 lint and format both run clean on the domain module with a broad select (E, F, I, UP, B, SIM, ANN, RUF). Nothing subtle.

GOTCHAS
- SQLFLUFF RULE VERDICTS — the deliverable. AL09 (aliasing.self_alias.column): CONFIGURE OFF. It fires on `o.order_id AS order_id`, which is precisely the 'alias every column of one fixed column list with AS' discipline that makes UNION ALL branches positionally safe. Removing the alias to satisfy AL09 would delete the i
- RF06 (references.quoting) 'Unnecessary quoted identifier': CONFIGURE OFF. Fires on every mixed-case identifier crossing from the business layer ("OrderPurchaseTs", "Stereotype") — six hits in a six-column view. It correctly leaves `dab."order"` alone. Note the subtlety: DuckDB is case-PRESERVING for unquoted identifier
- LT05 (layout.long_lines, default max 80) and LT09 (layout.select_targets): CONFIGURE OFF (or raise LT05 hard). A generator that emits one SELECT per line hits LT05 at 391 chars. Even a pretty-printing generator will blow 80 on `cast(x AS DECIMAL(28, 8)) AS long_business_column_name`. Set max_line_length = 120 AND exclu
- CV11 (convention.casting_style): FIX THE GENERATOR. Default policy is `consistent`, so mixing `cast()` and `::` in one file fails. Set `preferred_type_casting_style = cast` and make the generator emit `cast()` exclusively. `sqlfluff fix` auto-repairs this, so it is cheap either way.
- RF02 (references.qualification) 'Unqualified reference in select with more than one referenced table': FIX THE GENERATOR — and it is the one rule sqlfluff CANNOT auto-fix ('2 unfixable linting violations found'). Any join-producing generator (view_<entity>_with_rel, view_<src>_<rel>_<tgt>) must table-qualify every colu
- LT14 (layout.keyword_newline): FIX THE GENERATOR, but for free — `sqlfluff fix` repairs it automatically. Just run `sqlfluff fix` as a generation post-step rather than teaching the generator about newlines.
- yamllint walks into .venv/ by default and floods on third-party YAML (chardet ships a 2900-line training_metadata.yaml). `ignore: .venv/` in .yamllint.yaml is mandatory, or use `ignore-from-file: .gitignore`.
- yamllint default line-length is 80 and the brief specifies ~150-char contract lines. `allow-non-breakable-inline-mappings: true` is what makes the short flow mappings `{source_path: ..., target_name: ..., type: INTEGER}` survive when they overrun — set it alongside max: 160.
- ty is 0.0.78 — pre-1.0, pre-release version numbering. It works and is fast, but pin it exactly in uv.lock and expect diagnostic names/severities to churn. There is no `strict = true`; strictness is `--error all` on the CLI. If ty churn becomes intolerable the fallback is mypy --strict, but nothing observed here argues
- ty --error all does NOT flag fully unannotated functions. If you rely on ty alone for 'strict', untyped defs slip through. Ruff's ANN ruleset (ANN001/ANN201) is what closes that gap — keep ANN in the ruff select list or the type gate has a hole.
- pre-commit's `ruff format` hook fails the run when it reformats a file ('files were modified by this hook'). That is expected pre-commit behaviour, but in CI it means the format hook is effectively a `--check`. Either accept the re-run, or use `ruff format --check` in the CI-only config.

OPEN
- Not tested: sqlfluff with `templater = jinja` or `dbt`. I set `templater = raw` because the generator emits literal SQL. If any SQL in the repo carries Jinja (dlt or a dar__uss template), the raw templater will produce PRS errors on `{{ }}` and the config needs a per-path override.
- Not tested: DuckDB-specific syntax beyond QUALIFY — e.g. `SELECT * EXCLUDE (...)`, `SELECT * REPLACE (...)`, list/struct literals, `FROM tbl SELECT ...` (FROM-first), or `PIVOT`. The duckdb dialect inherits from postgres and may not cover all of these; worth a 5-minute probe before committing to sql
- Not tested: whether marimo notebook .py files survive ruff format and ty. marimo cells are decorated functions in a generated file; `@app.cell` functions typically lack return annotations and would trip ANN201, and marimo rewrites the file on save which fights ruff format. This needs its own probe —
- Not tested: pytest against a real DuckDB file (no duckdb package was installed). Only a pure-python unit test ran.
- Not measured: wall-clock cost of `sqlfluff lint` over a large generated-SQL tree. sqlfluff is the slowest of these by a wide margin; if the DAR generator emits hundreds of views, the pre-commit hook may need `--processes` or to be CI-only.
- Not tested: a CI runner invoking these without a HOME writable for pre-commit's cache. I had to set HOME=$PWD/.pchome to run pre-commit in this sandbox; on a normal runner HOME exists, but the `repo: local` design means the cache holds almost nothing anyway.

input.argument:
## Why an event-grained bridge at all Start with the thing that is actually in dispute. The corpus argues for two DAR shapes and never reconciles them: `consumption-layer-generates-itself` says generate a USS, `why-we-built-daana` says "dimensional modeling remains the natural choice for the DAR layer", and `ai-assisted-data-engineering` describes a Kimball agent building "dimensions, facts, snapshots" with conformed dimensions. The blog-synthesis names this "the single biggest unresolved conflict". So the USS is not handed to us; it is chosen. It is chosen because of what slice 2 will look like. **Generated Kimball star per business process** is a genuinely strong option and deserves better than dismissal: each fact has one explicit grain, there are no NULL-heavy wide rows, `count(*)` on a fact means something, every BI tool on earth expects it, and blueprint R2 is satisfied natively because each product owns its star. What it costs is exactly the tax the blog itemises: the unit of work becomes one star per question, so cost scales with questions rather than with model changes; "which fact table" returns; and — decisively for this build — two processes measured on different dates cannot be put on one timeline without a conformed date dimension, which is shared structure and therefore the same R2 deviation we are already registering, only with more moving parts. We would pay D-0001's price and not get the thing D-0001 buys. **One Big Table per question** is the cheapest thing that could work and is the honest baseline for slice 1: one flat table, no joins, marimo reads it, done in an afternoon. It fails at question two. Every attribute is duplicated per question, every definition change touches N tables, and the blog's own projection diagram puts OBT downstream of the USS ("obt = flatten the row") precisely because generating it from the bridge is a selection rather than a build. Keep it as a future projection, not as the primary shape. **Hand-written SQL per question** is the option nobody argues for and everybody does. For slice 1 it is fifteen lines and strictly less code than a generator. It is rejected on blueprint R4 ("Nothing here is hand-written or hand-edited") and on the thing R4 protects: a hand-written consumption layer has no sliceability contract, so "which questions does this model answer" becomes faith rather than a lookup, and the blog's whole coverage claim evaporates. **Entity-grained bridge** (one row per order carrying `placed_on`, `shipped_on`, `required_on` as three date columns) deserves a real hearing because it makes cohort questions trivial and keeps `count(*)` meaningful. It fails the one requirement the post treats as load-bearing: "Instead of one row per entity instance, you make the bridge event-based: one row per measurement event, each carrying its own date... One calendar, every process." With three date columns you need three joins to one calendar or three calendars, and "what happened in Q1 across orders, shipments and returns" is back to stitching. Event grain is the thing that earns the single calendar. **Puppini-canonical bridge — Stage plus keys only, measures left on the peripherals** — is the strongest rejected option, and it is arguably more faithful to the book than the blog is. It keeps the bridge narrow and stable: adding a measure changes a peripheral, not the structure every consumer reads. The blog explicitly departs from it ("It holds all the relations and all the measures in one place"; `SUM(b._measure__order_line__revenue) FROM _bridge b`), but "the blog said so" is not an argument. The argument is that a measure on a peripheral sits at *entity* grain, and an entity-grained measure cannot be dated by two different events. Revenue measured at placement and revenue measured at shipment are two numbers on two dates; on a peripheral there is one row and one place to put it. Once the bridge is event-grained, measures must live on the event row. Measures-on-bridge is not a stylistic preference, it is forced by the grain. ## 1. Fan-out: what propagates, and what the diagram already told us The post's sentence and the post's diagram disagree, and the disagreement is the whole problem. The sentence: "follow the relationships that go from many to one and inherit the keys **and measures** of everything you reach." The diagram immediately below it: walking n:1 from three lines to one order and summing the order's revenue gives 100, "counted once"; copying the order's 100 down onto the three lines gives 300, "fan-out, ×3". But copying the parent's measure onto every child row *is* the second picture. If "inherit the measures" meant "copy the values down", the safe walk would produce the unsafe number. The reading that makes the post coherent — and the decision here — is that **keys propagate and measure values do not propagate at all**. Precisely, for a stage rooted at entity E: - `E_key` is present and non-null. This is the row's own identity. - For every entity P reachable from E by a path made only of many-to-one edges, `P_key` is present, obtained by LEFT JOIN along the relationship views, and nullable where the relationship is optional. This is the downward propagation. - For any entity C on the one-to-many side of E, `C_key` is **never** present. There is no upward propagation; that direction is the fan. - Measures declared on (E, event) carry their value. **Every other measure column in the bridge is a typed NULL on these rows.** What a child inherits from a parent is therefore not the parent's measure but the parent's *dimensionality*: because the order-line rows carry `customer_key`, the order line's own measures become sliceable by customer attributes. Sliceability is the transitive closure of key inheritance. Measure values have no closure. That single sentence is the whole content of "cascading inheritance", stated so it cannot be implemented wrongly, and it is what makes the sliceability contract mechanically derivable: measure *m* owned by stage *S* is sliceable by key *k* exactly when *S* populates *k*. Nothing else needs deciding. The corollary, and it is not free: a *parent's* measure is not sliceable by a *child's* attribute. `placed_orders_count` cannot be broken down by product, ever, because the order-placed stage has no `product_key` and must not acquire one. The blog admits this class ("distinct counts across the wrong grain... you still have to think") without saying it out loud. The sliceability contract has to publish the absence, or the first analyst to want orders-by-product will discover it by getting a wrong number somewhere else. **The tests that prove it.** Three, and they are generated, not hand-written: *Ownership.* For each measure column, `count(*) WHERE IS NOT NULL AND (_stage, _event) <> (owner)` must be 0. This is the direct mechanical assertion that no measure value has propagated anywhere. It fails the day somebody "helpfully" fills a NULL. *Grain.* Each stage's row count equals the count of rows in its driving DAB view after the event-date filter and the version collapse. A LEFT JOIN along a relationship that turned out not to be many-to-one shows up here as a row count that is too high — which is the fan-out arriving through the key path rather than the measure path. *Join safety.* `_bridge LEFT JOIN USING (_key)` must have exactly the row count of `_bridge`, and every peripheral must satisfy `count(*) = count(DISTINCT _key)`. This is where a Kimball fan trap would actually materialise — at the consumer's join, not in the bridge — and it is why the peripheral is defined as one row per key rather than as the history view. The already-decided "computed twice from `das__staged` and from `dar__uss`" check sits on top of these and catches everything else. It is worth being honest about its limit: both computations express the same version-collapse rule, so it does not independently validate that rule. What it does validate is that the DAB mapping, the walk, the event filter and the peripheral join together reproduce a number derived from parquet the DAB layer never touched. That is worth a great deal, and it is not everything. ## 2. History: two stage kinds, one source view daana gives us `view_` (current, one row per key), `view__hist` (one row per value-run, dated `eff_tmstp`), and `view___`. The temptation is to read `view_` for events and `view__hist` for history. That is wrong in a way that only shows up later, for two reasons. First, `view_` carries no `eff_tmstp` and no `ver_tmstp` — spike 2 observed its column list as `ORDER_key` plus attributes only. A bridge built on it has no per-row provenance at all, which fails blueprint R5 and leaves no way to answer "which extraction produced this row". Second, and more important: by the earlier decision, DAB history is dated by `extracted_at`. So `eff_tmstp` is *when we saw it*, not *when it was true*. The `_hist` timeline is an **observation** timeline. That single fact settles the shape of the answer. A question about something that *happened* is dated by a business date attribute the model declares. A question about a state *as observed* is dated by `eff_tmstp`. There is no third thing in this system — business validity intervals simply do not exist unless a business date attribute carries them — and a design that pretends otherwise will produce confident nonsense. So: **every stage reads `view__hist`**, and the two kinds differ by one line. - A **transaction stage** adds `QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY eff_tmstp DESC) = 1`, collapsing to the version currently in effect. One row per instance per event. `_event_date` is the declared business date. `_is_current` is TRUE. `_observed_at` is the extraction that produced that version. - A **state stage** omits the QUALIFY and emits every version, `_event_date = cast(eff_tmstp AS DATE)` — the observation date — and `_is_current` computed by the same window. It answers "as we knew it on date D". `view_` and `view__with_rel` are never read at all. The current view is exactly the transaction stage's QUALIFY, and `with_rel` is useless (see below), so reading them buys nothing and costs a second code path. Two consequences to swallow. Because the transaction stage takes the *latest* version, a restated order date silently moves an order to a different month, and last quarter's answer changes. That is the correct behaviour — it is the corrected truth — but it means "reproducible" here means "reproducible from a given DAB state", not "frozen". The alternative, taking the earliest version (`ORDER BY eff_tmstp ASC`), gives as-first-observed and is defensible; it is rejected because it makes every correction invisible, which is worse. And peripherals are current-state, so joining them gives *current* attributes even to a historical bridge row — a Type-1 dimension by construction. "Ship country as it was recorded then" needs a state stage, and slice 1 does not have one. Slice 1 emits only a transaction stage. `_is_current` is therefore constant TRUE in slice 1, and that is deliberate: the column has to exist before the first state stage, because a consumer who writes `WHERE _is_current` must get the right answer on both kinds. conventions.md §1.3 already names `_is_current` as a structural column, which is itself evidence that the intended design has non-current rows on the bridge — a bridge that is current-only would have no use for it. ## 3. Where the relationship keys come from Spike 2 removes two of the three obvious answers by observation. `view__with_rel` carries no relationship keys at all: "DESCRIBE dab.view_ORDER_with_rel: ORDER_key | order_id | order_status | order_purchase_ts | order_value_amount | order_value_currency [6 rows] ... (no CUSTOMER_key column)". Its column list is byte-identical to `view_ORDER`. The name promises denormalised foreign keys and delivers nothing. `_focal` and `_idfr` are created and never populated on DuckDB: "CUSTOMER_focal 0 / CUSTOMER_idfr 0 / CUSTOMER_desc 25 / ORDER_CUSTOMER_x 3", while `view_CUSTOMER` still returns the correct three rows. A generator that joins `_focal` or `_idfr` — which is what you would design if you had only seen the PostgreSQL run — produces empty results with no error. That leaves `view___` (`ORDER_key`, `CUSTOMER_key`, `type_key`, `eff_tmstp`, `ver_tmstp`) as the only place a relationship key exists. So: **`_key` is obtained by LEFT JOINing `view___

` on `_key`, and transitively along the path.** LEFT, not INNER: an order with no customer must still appear, or the measure total changes and the grain test catches it as a defect that is really a join. The independent architectural argument matters as much as the empirical one, because it survives the vendor fixing the DuckDB defect. `_desc`, `_x`, `_idfr` and `_focal` are daana's physical implementation; the `view_*` layer is its published interface. `integration-by-design-analytical-identifiers` is explicit that "DAR joins only on `{ENTITY}_key`; the `_idfr` table is an integration mechanism, not a reporting dimension — downstream tables see the result, not the resolution." And 0.7.0 already broke downstream consumers once by lower-casing framework column names. Building DAR on the physical tables is a dependency on internals that have a demonstrated history of moving. **The generator reads YAML, not the catalog.** It is a pure function of `dab/model.yaml` and `dab/uss.yaml`, and it never introspects the database. Three reasons. Generation must work before deploy, or the ADR-before-code discipline has nothing to review. DuckDB preserves the model's casing (`view_CUSTOMER`, not `view_customer`), so any code that string-matches `information_schema` breaks — spike 2's gotcha — while code that renders names from the model is right by construction. And conventions.md §5 forbids data vocabulary under `src/` and in tests: a generator that maps YAML to SQL text can be unit-tested against a neutral fixture model, so the tests *prove* the machinery is generic; a generator that introspects DuckDB cannot be tested without a warehouse and cannot avoid naming real entities. **Cardinality is the hole.** model.yaml declares `source_entity_id`, `target_entity_id`, `name`, `definition` — and no cardinality. The entire walk is a function of cardinality. Three ways out. Declaring cardinality in `dab/uss.yaml` gives a second home for a modelling fact and invites the drift blueprint B8 exists to prevent. Inferring nothing and refusing to walk makes the USS pointless. The choice here is to **assume source→target is many-to-one and make the assumption falsifiable at build time**: conventions.md §1.2 already requires relationship names to read as a sentence source→target (`ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER`), which asserts the direction, and spike 2 observed exactly one row per `ORDER_key` in the relationship view. The generator emits, per walked edge, a guard: `count(*) = count(DISTINCT _key)` in `view___`, and the build fails if it does not hold. The blog says the generator "skips it and tells you"; a warning in a log is not telling anyone, so the guard fails the build and the only escape is an explicit `exclude_relationships` entry in `dab/uss.yaml` naming the edge and the reason. That is the warning made durable and reviewed. The cost is real: the day someone models a legitimate many-to-many relationship in DAB — which daana 0.7.0 now supports first-class — DAR generation stops until a human writes that entry. ## Event dates, and the order that never shipped The event date is **declared, never inferred**. Each event in `dab/uss.yaml` names the entity attribute that dates it. Inference from "the only date-typed attribute" dies immediately on Northwind Orders, which has three. Using DAB's `eff_tmstp` for everything would silently turn "orders per order month" into "orders per load month" — a wrong answer that looks entirely plausible, which is the failure mode the blueprint calls coherent-looking incoherence. Reusing DMDL's `START_TIMESTAMP` type is tempting because it is already in model.yaml, but that type declares a validity-interval role, not a measurement event, and three dates would need three roles it does not have. An entity row whose event date is null **does not produce a bridge row**. The stage's SELECT carries `WHERE IS NOT NULL`. The reasoning is that the bridge's grain is one row per measurement event, and an event that did not occur is not a measurement event: emitting a row for an unshipped order and setting `shipped_orders_count = 1` on it makes "shipped orders" count orders that never shipped. The two alternatives were weighed honestly. A sentinel calendar member (the Kimball unknown-date trick) preserves `count(*)` per stage and makes "unshipped" a filter, but it stops the calendar being a calendar and puts a non-date in every time series. Coalescing to the entity's primary date fabricates a shipment in a month where none happened. The cost is specific and someone will trip over it: **"orders not yet shipped" is not a row count anywhere.** It is `sum(placed) − sum(shipped)` over the same period, or a separately declared measure on the placed stage. That is the same shape as conventions.md §2's rule that ratios are not stored — store the additive parts, combine at query time — so it is at least a familiar discipline rather than a new one. ## Measures, and why the event is the qualifier `dab/uss.yaml` measures are either `count` (the generator emits `cast(1 AS BIGINT)`) or `sum` of one named DAB attribute. **There is no free-text SQL in uss.yaml and no filter clause.** This is the rule that keeps first-time business logic out of DAR, and it has a consequence that turns out to be the deepest thing in the design: a measure that "needs a WHERE" is a different *event*. "Shipped orders" is not "placed orders with a filter"; it is the shipped stage. The event is the qualifier. That is why the bridge is event-based, and it connects straight back to `anatomy-of-business-question`'s anatomy — measure, dimensions, time grain — where the measure and its qualifier are one thing, not a metric plus an ad-hoc predicate. Every measure is additive at the bridge grain, so `sum()` is always the correct aggregate and `count(*)` is never a measure. `count(*)` over the bridge counts events of every kind mixed together and is meaningless — a permanent hazard, mitigated by the contract publishing which stage owns what, not removed by it. ## Files, and whether generated SQL is committed Generated SQL is **committed**, and CI regenerates and fails on any diff. This looks like it contradicts R4 ("Nothing here is hand-written or hand-edited") and in fact enforces it: the drift check turns "nobody edits generated output" from an aspiration into a failing test. The blog-synthesis lists "whether generated SQL is a reviewed surface" as unresolved in the corpus, so this is decided here rather than inherited. The affirmative argument is that the diff of the generated SQL *is* the review surface for a model change — the blueprint's own warning is that "Generation guarantees consistency, not correctness", and the diff is the only place a human sees what a one-line YAML change did to the layer every page reads. conventions.md §3 pushes the same way ("SQL that lives in a Python string is written to a file so the same linter sees it"). The cost is diff noise: a small model change can rewrite `_bridge.sql` wholesale, and reviewers learn to skim it, which is exactly how the review surface stops working. Generation runs `sqlfluff fix` as a post-step rather than teaching the generator about line layout — spike 4's recommendation, and it means the committed file and the regenerated file are byte-identical by construction. ## On conventions.md §1.3 Obeyed as written: `_measure____`, `

## Files the generator emits (all committed under `dar/uss/`)

```
dar/uss/_bridge.sql        CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dar__uss._bridge      (UNION ALL of stages)
dar/uss/_calendar.sql      CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dar__uss._calendar
dar/uss/order.sql          CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dar__uss."order"      (one per entity)
dar/uss/checks.sql         one statement per invariant, each returning a violation count
dar/uss/sliceability.yaml  measure x key coverage contract (the pre-trust coverage report)
dar/uss/plan.yaml          objects in build order: peripherals -> _bridge -> _calendar
```

CLI: `uv run adss dar generate` (YAML -> files, no database, offline) · `uv run adss dar generate --check` (CI: regenerate, fail on any diff) · `uv run adss dar build` (execute `plan.yaml`) · `uv run adss dar check` (run `checks.sql`, every count must be 0).

## Input: `dab/uss.yaml` (slice 1)

```yaml
uss:
  events:
    - id: PLACED
      entity: ORDER
      definition: An order was placed, on the date the business records as its order date.
      date_attribute: PLACED_ON
      measures:
        - id: PLACED_ORDERS_COUNT
          definition: The number of orders placed, one per order, counted on the date it was placed.
          aggregate: count
  states: []
  exclude_relationships: []
```

`aggregate` is `count` (emits `cast(1 AS BIGINT)`) or `sum` with `attribute: <DAB_ATTRIBUTE>`. No SQL, no filters. Peripherals are derived from `model.yaml`, never declared.

## `dar__uss._bridge` — the complete column contract

| Column | Type | Null | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `_stage` | VARCHAR | no | the entity this row is a row *of*; equals the name of the peripheral whose key is guaranteed non-null here (`order`) |
| `_event` | VARCHAR | no | the event identifier, lower-cased (`placed`, `shipped`, `observed`) |
| `_event_date` | DATE | no | the date of the measurement event; joins `_calendar.date_key` |
| `_is_current` | BOOLEAN | no | TRUE if this row reflects the entity version currently in effect; always TRUE on a transaction stage |
| `_observed_at` | TIMESTAMP | no | DAB `eff_tmstp` of the version behind this row = DAS `extracted_at`; per-row provenance |
| `<entity>_key` | VARCHAR | own key: no; inherited: yes | one column per entity populated by at least one stage. Own key non-null; parent keys inherited along many-to-one edges; child keys never present |
| `_measure__<entity>__<measure>` | BIGINT for `count`, DECIMAL(28,8) for `sum` of a numeric attribute | non-null only on the owning stage | one column per declared measure. Non-owning branches emit `cast(NULL AS <T>)` |

Slice 1 instantiates: `_stage, _event, _event_date, _is_current, _observed_at, order_key, _measure__order__placed_orders_count`.

Rules the contract carries: every measure is additive at this grain, so `sum()` is always right and `count(*)` is never a measure. A join on the row's own `_stage` key may be INNER; a join on an inherited key must be LEFT. The column list grows additively with questions and is never narrowed.

## `dar__uss."order"` — peripheral (one per entity)

| Column | Type | Null | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `order_key` | VARCHAR | no | unique; the DAB business key value (`10248`) |
| `_observed_at` | TIMESTAMP | no | `eff_tmstp` of the current version |
| `order_id`, `order_status`, `order_ship_country`, … | VARCHAR / TIMESTAMP / DECIMAL(28,8) | yes | one per declared attribute, lower-cased attribute id unchanged |

Current-state, exactly one row per key. No `_is_current` (it could never vary). No `_stage`.

## `dar__uss._calendar` — the complete column contract

| Column | Type | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `date_key` | DATE | `1996-07-04` |
| `year_number` | INTEGER | `1996` |

Dense daily rows from `min(_event_date)` to `max(_event_date)` over the whole bridge — a calendar containing only dates that occurred is not a calendar, and a month with no orders must still appear in a time series. Civil arithmetic only: no fiscal periods, no holidays, no ISO weeks. Those are business meaning and belong in DAB (blueprint B8), not invented by a generator.

## Worked example — the single transaction stage, house style

`dar/uss/_bridge.sql` (verified: executes on duckdb 1.5.5, lints clean under the repo's `.sqlfluff`)

```sql
-- Generated by `uv run adss dar generate`. Do not edit; edit dab/uss.yaml and regenerate.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dar__uss._bridge AS
WITH order_placed AS (
    SELECT
        o."ORDER_key" AS order_key,
        o.eff_tmstp AS observed_at,
        cast(o."PLACED_ON" AS DATE) AS event_date
    FROM dab."view_ORDER_hist" AS o
    WHERE o."PLACED_ON" IS NOT NULL
    QUALIFY row_number() OVER (
        PARTITION BY o."ORDER_key"
        ORDER BY o.eff_tmstp DESC
    ) = 1
)

SELECT
    'order' AS _stage,
    'placed' AS _event,
    op.event_date AS _event_date,
    TRUE AS _is_current,
    op.observed_at AS _observed_at,
    op.order_key AS order_key,
    cast(1 AS BIGINT) AS _measure__order__placed_orders_count
FROM order_placed AS op;
```

A second stage is a second CTE plus a `UNION ALL` branch that emits `cast(NULL AS BIGINT) AS _measure__order__placed_orders_count` and `cast(1 AS BIGINT) AS _measure__order__shipped_orders_count`. Verified end to end on three synthetic hist rows: placed total 2, shipped total 1, `count(*)` 3, ownership violations 0 — the unshipped order correctly has no shipment row.

Note the shape: `WHERE` before `QUALIFY` means the version collapse picks the latest version *in which the event is dated*. Mixed-case DAB identifiers are double-quoted (`"ORDER_key"`, `"PLACED_ON"`); lower-case framework columns (`eff_tmstp`) are not, because §3's quoting rule exists to make a mixed-case identifier's quotes visible. `QUALIFY` is why `.sqlfluff` must use the duckdb dialect.

## `dar/uss/_calendar.sql`

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dar__uss._calendar AS
WITH bounds AS (
    SELECT
        min(b._event_date) AS first_date,
        max(b._event_date) AS last_date
    FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b
),

calendar_day AS (
    SELECT
        cast(d.day_ts AS DATE) AS date_key
    FROM bounds AS bo,
        range(bo.first_date, bo.last_date + INTERVAL 1 DAY, INTERVAL 1 DAY) AS d (day_ts)
)

SELECT
    cd.date_key AS date_key,
    cast(year(cd.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS year_number,
    cast(quarter(cd.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS quarter_of_year,
    cast(month(cd.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS month_of_year,
    cast(day(cd.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS day_of_month,
    cast(date_trunc('year', cd.date_key) AS DATE) AS year_start,
    cast(date_trunc('quarter', cd.date_key) AS DATE) AS quarter_start,
    cast(date_trunc('month', cd.date_key) AS DATE) AS month_start,
    strftime(cd.date_key, '%Y') || '-Q' || cast(quarter(cd.date_key) AS VARCHAR) AS quarter_label,
    strftime(cd.date_key, '%Y-%m') AS month_label
FROM calendar_day AS cd;
```

## The slice-1 question against the contract

```sql
SELECT
    c.month_start AS month_start,
    o.order_ship_country AS order_ship_country,
    sum(b._measure__order__placed_orders_count) AS placed_orders_count
FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b
INNER JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS c ON b._event_date = c.date_key
INNER JOIN dar__uss."order" AS o ON b.order_key = o.order_key
WHERE b._event = 'placed'
GROUP BY c.month_start, o.order_ship_country
ORDER BY c.month_start, o.order_ship_country;
```

Lints clean. The marimo page casts the aggregate to DOUBLE before charting — spike 3 observed that DuckDB DECIMAL reaches polars as `decimal[38,0]` and altair cannot encode it; the cast belongs in the page, not in the bridge, so the bridge keeps DAB's precision.
