consequences.text: Additivity stops being a discipline and becomes a build-time property that a generated check asserts. The ownership invariant (`a measure column is non-null only on its owning stage`) is one line of SQL per measure and it fails the moment anyone copies a parent measure down a relationship, which is the single most common way a consumption layer starts double-counting.

Every process lands on one dense calendar, so a question spanning placement and shipment is one GROUP BY rather than a union of two stars. This is the thing the event grain buys, and it is the reason the shared-structure deviation D-0001 is worth its price.

The next question costs a marimo page, not a model. Adding an entity, an event or a measure is a new stage or a new column — additive in DAR the way blueprint B7 is additive in DAB — and every existing page keeps working because nothing it names changes.

Coverage is inspectable before anyone trusts it. `sliceability.yaml` is derived mechanically from the same walk that builds the bridge, so `can I break this measure down by that key` is a lookup, and the absences (orders by product, for instance) are published rather than discovered by getting a wrong number.

Reading only `view_<E>_hist` and `view_<S>_<REL>_<T>` keeps DAR off daana's physical internals — `_desc`, `_x`, `_idfr`, `_focal`, the DuckDB table macros — which 0.7.0 has already demonstrated it is willing to change underneath downstream consumers.

The generator is a pure function of two YAML files, so it unit-tests against a neutral fixture model with no warehouse and no data vocabulary in `src/` or in tests, which is what conventions §5 asks for and what proves the machinery is source-agnostic rather than asserting it.

The column contract is a public API with no deprecation path. Every page names `_measure__order__placed_orders_count` and `order_key` literally. Renaming a measure in `dab/uss.yaml` renames a column and breaks every consumer at once; there is no aliasing view layer and no per-reader projection (that is exactly what D-0001 gave up). The first measure rename is the day this cost is paid, and it will be paid in full.

`count(*)` on the bridge is meaningless and it is the most natural thing an analyst will type. The bridge mixes events of different kinds on different dates, so its row count is neither the number of orders nor the number of shipments — the two-stage worked example gives 2 placed, 1 shipped, and `count(*)` = 3. The sliceability contract mitigates this; it does not remove it, and no amount of documentation will stop it happening in a PivotTable.

An entity whose event date is null produces no row, so `orders not yet shipped` is not a row count anywhere in the system. It is `sum(placed) - sum(shipped)` over a period, or a separately declared measure. Somebody will count rows in the shipped stage, subtract from an order total taken at a different grain, and be wrong in a way that looks arithmetically fine.

Full rebuild only. The blog's incremental recipe (`WHERE ver_tmstp > last_run_tmstp`, plus a persisted watermark) is not implementable on the view contract spike 2 observed: `ver_tmstp` appears on `view_<S>_<REL>_<T>` and on neither `view_<E>` nor `view_<E>_hist`. At Northwind scale this is free; it is a wall at any real volume, and the fix requires either a daana change or reading `_desc` directly, which this record forbids.

Materialising DAR does not decouple readers from the DAB rebuild, because it is one DuckDB file. Spike 2 observed that any other open connection — including a read-only one — makes `daana-cli execute` fail with the actively misleading error `daana framework is not installed on the remote database`. The marimo page must be stopped for every build, and whoever operates it has to be told that this error means the file is busy.

Peripheral attributes are current-state, so joining them gives today's values to a historical bridge row. Slice 1's answer per ship country will move retroactively if a source restates ShipCountry, and `as it was recorded then` is not answerable until a state stage exists. This is a Type-1 dimension by construction, chosen deliberately, and it is the kind of thing that is discovered during an audit rather than during development.

A many-to-many relationship added in DAB stops DAR generation. daana 0.7.0 supports M:N first-class; the cardinality guard fails the build and the only escape is an explicit `exclude_relationships` entry. That is the right failure — silent fan-out is worse — but it means a DAB modeller can block the DAR build with a change that is perfectly valid in their own layer.

Committing generated SQL means a one-line YAML change can rewrite `_bridge.sql` wholesale. The diff is meant to be the review surface for model changes; a diff that is large and mechanical every time is a diff reviewers learn to skim, which is precisely how a review surface stops working.

The bridge is wide and sparse by construction: with k entities and m measures every stage emits mostly NULLs. Harmless at this scale, and the largest object in the file at any other. The wide-table cost the blueprint warns about in DAB reappears here — deliberately, because DAR is allowed to be shaped for consumption, but it is still real.

DAR is the layer every consumer is written against, and this record fixes the column names those consumers will type. `_measure__order__placed_orders_count` is not an implementation detail; it is the string in the marimo page, in the second page, and in whatever reads this warehouse in year three. Blueprint R4 makes the layer regenerable but gives no deprecation path: regeneration under a changed contract does not migrate a consumer, it breaks one. So the cost of getting this wrong is not rework in DAR, it is rework in everything downstream of DAR, forever, and slice 1 exercises almost none of it — one entity, one event, one count, no relationships. Nearly every column being fixed here will be unexercised and permanent on the day it lands.

The obvious answer — "generate the Unified Star Schema the blog describes" — is not available as written, because the blog contradicts itself on the one point that matters most. `consumption-layer-generates-itself` says the walk follows many-to-one edges and inherits "the keys **and measures** of everything you reach". The diagram directly beneath that sentence shows three order lines rolling up to one order: the safe n:1 walk gives `sum(order.revenue) = 100`, "counted once", while pushing the order's 100 down onto each of its three lines gives 300, "fan-out, ×3". But copying a parent's measure onto every child row *is* the second picture. If measures propagated the way the sentence says, the safe walk would produce the unsafe number. The post's own worked example refutes its own rule, and no reading of the post resolves it. That has to be resolved here, precisely, because "inherit everything along it" implemented literally is a silent doubling.

The second difficulty is that daana's published interface does not contain the things a USS generator naturally reaches for, and spike 2 established this by observation rather than inference. `view_<entity>_with_rel` — the object whose name promises denormalised foreign keys — carries none: its column list is byte-identical to `view_<entity>`, with no `CUSTOMER_key` on `view_ORDER_with_rel`. `<entity>_focal` and `<entity>_idfr` are created and never populated on DuckDB (0 rows each, while `CUSTOMER_desc` holds 25 and the views still return correct results), so a generator designed against the PostgreSQL run joins them and silently returns nothing. And `model.yaml` declares relationships with only `source_entity_id`, `target_entity_id`, `name` and `definition` — **no cardinality at all** — while the entire many-to-one walk is a function of cardinality. The one input the generator most needs does not exist in the model it must read.

The third difficulty is what "history" means in this system, and it is not what the USS literature assumes. By the prior decision, DAB history is dated by `extracted_at` — `eff_tmstp` is `to_timestamp(cast(_dlt_load_id AS DOUBLE))`. So the `view_<E>_hist` timeline is an **observation** timeline: when we saw a value, not when it was true. Business validity intervals do not exist in this warehouse unless a business date attribute carries them. That means a question about something that *happened* and a question about a state *as observed* are dated by two entirely different clocks, and a bridge that conflates them will answer "how many orders were placed in July 1996" with a number that moves whenever we reload.

Fourth, the corpus does not agree that a USS is even the right shape. `why-we-built-daana` says "dimensional modeling remains the natural choice for the DAR layer"; `ai-assisted-data-engineering` describes an agent building Kimball facts, dimensions and snapshots with conformed dimensions; `consumption-layer-generates-itself` says stop sorting tables into facts and dimensions altogether. The blog-synthesis names this "the single biggest unresolved conflict" in eighteen posts. And even within the USS post, the build target is written `order_line.bridge` (per entity) while the sample SQL queries a single `_bridge`, with no explanation of the relationship — and that sample SQL selects `t.territory_key` with no `t` anywhere in its `FROM`.

Finally, the escape hatches are already spent. Deviation D-0001 is registered and open: there is one shared `dar__uss`, no per-consumer projection, and its own cost entry says "there is no per-reader projection, so 'this reader may not see freight' cannot be expressed" and "two readers cannot hold different definitions of the same measure". Whatever contract this record fixes is the contract for every consumer simultaneously, with no room to differ.

It genuinely validates the DAB mapping and the walk against parquet DAB never touched; it does not independently validate the collapse rule itself.

How a business calendar (fiscal periods, holidays) enters the system. This record forbids the generator from inventing one — that is business meaning and B8 puts it in DAB — but whether DAB models a CALENDAR_DAY entity that the walk reaches, or the calendar gains a declared mapping, is unresolved and the first fiscal-quarter request will force it.

Whether measures declared in dab/uss.yaml stay reusable. B6 forbids anything in DAB existing because one consumer wanted it; a measure declared for a page is exactly that. The rule here is that uss.yaml declares business measures and events and nothing page-specific, but there is no check that enforces it, and a per-page section appearing in uss.yaml is the observable sign B6 has broken.

data.argument:
## Why an event-grained bridge at all Start with the thing that is actually in dispute. The corpus argues for two DAR shapes and never reconciles them: `consumption-layer-generates-itself` says generate a USS, `why-we-built-daana` says "dimensional modeling remains the natural choice for the DAR layer", and `ai-assisted-data-engineering` describes a Kimball agent building "dimensions, facts, snapshots" with conformed dimensions. The blog-synthesis names this "the single biggest unresolved conflict". So the USS is not handed to us; it is chosen. It is chosen because of what slice 2 will look like. **Generated Kimball star per business process** is a genuinely strong option and deserves better than dismissal: each fact has one explicit grain, there are no NULL-heavy wide rows, `count(*)` on a fact means something, every BI tool on earth expects it, and blueprint R2 is satisfied natively because each product owns its star. What it costs is exactly the tax the blog itemises: the unit of work becomes one star per question, so cost scales with questions rather than with model changes; "which fact table" returns; and — decisively for this build — two processes measured on different dates cannot be put on one timeline without a conformed date dimension, which is shared structure and therefore the same R2 deviation we are already registering, only with more moving parts. We would pay D-0001's price and not get the thing D-0001 buys. **One Big Table per question** is the cheapest thing that could work and is the honest baseline for slice 1: one flat table, no joins, marimo reads it, done in an afternoon. It fails at question two. Every attribute is duplicated per question, every definition change touches N tables, and the blog's own projection diagram puts OBT downstream of the USS ("obt = flatten the row") precisely because generating it from the bridge is a selection rather than a build. Keep it as a future projection, not as the primary shape. **Hand-written SQL per question** is the option nobody argues for and everybody does. For slice 1 it is fifteen lines and strictly less code than a generator. It is rejected on blueprint R4 ("Nothing here is hand-written or hand-edited") and on the thing R4 protects: a hand-written consumption layer has no sliceability contract, so "which questions does this model answer" becomes faith rather than a lookup, and the blog's whole coverage claim evaporates. **Entity-grained bridge** (one row per order carrying `placed_on`, `shipped_on`, `required_on` as three date columns) deserves a real hearing because it makes cohort questions trivial and keeps `count(*)` meaningful. It fails the one requirement the post treats as load-bearing: "Instead of one row per entity instance, you make the bridge event-based: one row per measurement event, each carrying its own date... One calendar, every process." With three date columns you need three joins to one calendar or three calendars, and "what happened in Q1 across orders, shipments and returns" is back to stitching. Event grain is the thing that earns the single calendar. **Puppini-canonical bridge — Stage plus keys only, measures left on the peripherals** — is the strongest rejected option, and it is arguably more faithful to the book than the blog is. It keeps the bridge narrow and stable: adding a measure changes a peripheral, not the structure every consumer reads. The blog explicitly departs from it ("It holds all the relations and all the measures in one place"; `SUM(b._measure__order_line__revenue) FROM _bridge b`), but "the blog said so" is not an argument. The argument is that a measure on a peripheral sits at *entity* grain, and an entity-grained measure cannot be dated by two different events. Revenue measured at placement and revenue measured at shipment are two numbers on two dates; on a peripheral there is one row and one place to put it. Once the bridge is event-grained, measures must live on the event row. Measures-on-bridge is not a stylistic preference, it is forced by the grain. ## 1. Fan-out: what propagates, and what the diagram already told us The post's sentence and the post's diagram disagree, and the disagreement is the whole problem. The sentence: "follow the relationships that go from many to one and inherit the keys **and measures** of everything you reach." The diagram immediately below it: walking n:1 from three lines to one order and summing the order's revenue gives 100, "counted once"; copying the order's 100 down onto the three lines gives 300, "fan-out, ×3". But copying the parent's measure onto every child row *is* the second picture. If "inherit the measures" meant "copy the values down", the safe walk would produce the unsafe number. The reading that makes the post coherent — and the decision here — is that **keys propagate and measure values do not propagate at all**. Precisely, for a stage rooted at entity E: - `E_key` is present and non-null. This is the row's own identity. - For every entity P reachable from E by a path made only of many-to-one edges, `P_key` is present, obtained by LEFT JOIN along the relationship views, and nullable where the relationship is optional. This is the downward propagation. - For any entity C on the one-to-many side of E, `C_key` is **never** present. There is no upward propagation; that direction is the fan. - Measures declared on (E, event) carry their value. **Every other measure column in the bridge is a typed NULL on these rows.** What a child inherits from a parent is therefore not the parent's measure but the parent's *dimensionality*: because the order-line rows carry `customer_key`, the order line's own measures become sliceable by customer attributes. Sliceability is the transitive closure of key inheritance. Measure values have no closure. That single sentence is the whole content of "cascading inheritance", stated so it cannot be implemented wrongly, and it is what makes the sliceability contract mechanically derivable: measure *m* owned by stage *S* is sliceable by key *k* exactly when *S* populates *k*. Nothing else needs deciding. The corollary, and it is not free: a *parent's* measure is not sliceable by a *child's* attribute. `placed_orders_count` cannot be broken down by product, ever, because the order-placed stage has no `product_key` and must not acquire one. The blog admits this class ("distinct counts across the wrong grain... you still have to think") without saying it out loud. The sliceability contract has to publish the absence, or the first analyst to want orders-by-product will discover it by getting a wrong number somewhere else. **The tests that prove it.** Three, and they are generated, not hand-written: *Ownership.* For each measure column, `count(*) WHERE IS NOT NULL AND (_stage, _event) <> (owner)` must be 0. This is the direct mechanical assertion that no measure value has propagated anywhere. It fails the day somebody "helpfully" fills a NULL. *Grain.* Each stage's row count equals the count of rows in its driving DAB view after the event-date filter and the version collapse. A LEFT JOIN along a relationship that turned out not to be many-to-one shows up here as a row count that is too high — which is the fan-out arriving through the key path rather than the measure path. *Join safety.* `_bridge LEFT JOIN USING (_key)` must have exactly the row count of `_bridge`, and every peripheral must satisfy `count(*) = count(DISTINCT _key)`. This is where a Kimball fan trap would actually materialise — at the consumer's join, not in the bridge — and it is why the peripheral is defined as one row per key rather than as the history view. The already-decided "computed twice from `das__staged` and from `dar__uss`" check sits on top of these and catches everything else. It is worth being honest about its limit: both computations express the same version-collapse rule, so it does not independently validate that rule. What it does validate is that the DAB mapping, the walk, the event filter and the peripheral join together reproduce a number derived from parquet the DAB layer never touched. That is worth a great deal, and it is not everything. ## 2. History: two stage kinds, one source view daana gives us `view_` (current, one row per key), `view__hist` (one row per value-run, dated `eff_tmstp`), and `view___`. The temptation is to read `view_` for events and `view__hist` for history. That is wrong in a way that only shows up later, for two reasons. First, `view_` carries no `eff_tmstp` and no `ver_tmstp` — spike 2 observed its column list as `ORDER_key` plus attributes only. A bridge built on it has no per-row provenance at all, which fails blueprint R5 and leaves no way to answer "which extraction produced this row". Second, and more important: by the earlier decision, DAB history is dated by `extracted_at`. So `eff_tmstp` is *when we saw it*, not *when it was true*. The `_hist` timeline is an **observation** timeline. That single fact settles the shape of the answer. A question about something that *happened* is dated by a business date attribute the model declares. A question about a state *as observed* is dated by `eff_tmstp`. There is no third thing in this system — business validity intervals simply do not exist unless a business date attribute carries them — and a design that pretends otherwise will produce confident nonsense. So: **every stage reads `view__hist`**, and the two kinds differ by one line. - A **transaction stage** adds `QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY eff_tmstp DESC) = 1`, collapsing to the version currently in effect. One row per instance per event. `_event_date` is the declared business date. `_is_current` is TRUE. `_observed_at` is the extraction that produced that version. - A **state stage** omits the QUALIFY and emits every version, `_event_date = cast(eff_tmstp AS DATE)` — the observation date — and `_is_current` computed by the same window. It answers "as we knew it on date D". `view_` and `view__with_rel` are never read at all. The current view is exactly the transaction stage's QUALIFY, and `with_rel` is useless (see below), so reading them buys nothing and costs a second code path. Two consequences to swallow. Because the transaction stage takes the *latest* version, a restated order date silently moves an order to a different month, and last quarter's answer changes. That is the correct behaviour — it is the corrected truth — but it means "reproducible" here means "reproducible from a given DAB state", not "frozen". The alternative, taking the earliest version (`ORDER BY eff_tmstp ASC`), gives as-first-observed and is defensible; it is rejected because it makes every correction invisible, which is worse. And peripherals are current-state, so joining them gives *current* attributes even to a historical bridge row — a Type-1 dimension by construction. "Ship country as it was recorded then" needs a state stage, and slice 1 does not have one. Slice 1 emits only a transaction stage. `_is_current` is therefore constant TRUE in slice 1, and that is deliberate: the column has to exist before the first state stage, because a consumer who writes `WHERE _is_current` must get the right answer on both kinds. conventions.md §1.3 already names `_is_current` as a structural column, which is itself evidence that the intended design has non-current rows on the bridge — a bridge that is current-only would have no use for it. ## 3. Where the relationship keys come from Spike 2 removes two of the three obvious answers by observation. `view__with_rel` carries no relationship keys at all: "DESCRIBE dab.view_ORDER_with_rel: ORDER_key | order_id | order_status | order_purchase_ts | order_value_amount | order_value_currency [6 rows] ... (no CUSTOMER_key column)". Its column list is byte-identical to `view_ORDER`. The name promises denormalised foreign keys and delivers nothing. `_focal` and `_idfr` are created and never populated on DuckDB: "CUSTOMER_focal 0 / CUSTOMER_idfr 0 / CUSTOMER_desc 25 / ORDER_CUSTOMER_x 3", while `view_CUSTOMER` still returns the correct three rows. A generator that joins `_focal` or `_idfr` — which is what you would design if you had only seen the PostgreSQL run — produces empty results with no error. That leaves `view___` (`ORDER_key`, `CUSTOMER_key`, `type_key`, `eff_tmstp`, `ver_tmstp`) as the only place a relationship key exists. So: **`_key` is obtained by LEFT JOINing `view___

` on `_key`, and transitively along the path.** LEFT, not INNER: an order with no customer must still appear, or the measure total changes and the grain test catches it as a defect that is really a join. The independent architectural argument matters as much as the empirical one, because it survives the vendor fixing the DuckDB defect. `_desc`, `_x`, `_idfr` and `_focal` are daana's physical implementation; the `view_*` layer is its published interface. `integration-by-design-analytical-identifiers` is explicit that "DAR joins only on `{ENTITY}_key`; the `_idfr` table is an integration mechanism, not a reporting dimension — downstream tables see the result, not the resolution." And 0.7.0 already broke downstream consumers once by lower-casing framework column names. Building DAR on the physical tables is a dependency on internals that have a demonstrated history of moving. **The generator reads YAML, not the catalog.** It is a pure function of `dab/model.yaml` and `dab/uss.yaml`, and it never introspects the database. Three reasons. Generation must work before deploy, or the ADR-before-code discipline has nothing to review. DuckDB preserves the model's casing (`view_CUSTOMER`, not `view_customer`), so any code that string-matches `information_schema` breaks — spike 2's gotcha — while code that renders names from the model is right by construction. And conventions.md §5 forbids data vocabulary under `src/` and in tests: a generator that maps YAML to SQL text can be unit-tested against a neutral fixture model, so the tests *prove* the machinery is generic; a generator that introspects DuckDB cannot be tested without a warehouse and cannot avoid naming real entities. **Cardinality is the hole.** model.yaml declares `source_entity_id`, `target_entity_id`, `name`, `definition` — and no cardinality. The entire walk is a function of cardinality. Three ways out. Declaring cardinality in `dab/uss.yaml` gives a second home for a modelling fact and invites the drift blueprint B8 exists to prevent. Inferring nothing and refusing to walk makes the USS pointless. The choice here is to **assume source→target is many-to-one and make the assumption falsifiable at build time**: conventions.md §1.2 already requires relationship names to read as a sentence source→target (`ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER`), which asserts the direction, and spike 2 observed exactly one row per `ORDER_key` in the relationship view. The generator emits, per walked edge, a guard: `count(*) = count(DISTINCT _key)` in `view___`, and the build fails if it does not hold. The blog says the generator "skips it and tells you"; a warning in a log is not telling anyone, so the guard fails the build and the only escape is an explicit `exclude_relationships` entry in `dab/uss.yaml` naming the edge and the reason. That is the warning made durable and reviewed. The cost is real: the day someone models a legitimate many-to-many relationship in DAB — which daana 0.7.0 now supports first-class — DAR generation stops until a human writes that entry. ## Event dates, and the order that never shipped The event date is **declared, never inferred**. Each event in `dab/uss.yaml` names the entity attribute that dates it. Inference from "the only date-typed attribute" dies immediately on Northwind Orders, which has three. Using DAB's `eff_tmstp` for everything would silently turn "orders per order month" into "orders per load month" — a wrong answer that looks entirely plausible, which is the failure mode the blueprint calls coherent-looking incoherence. Reusing DMDL's `START_TIMESTAMP` type is tempting because it is already in model.yaml, but that type declares a validity-interval role, not a measurement event, and three dates would need three roles it does not have. An entity row whose event date is null **does not produce a bridge row**. The stage's SELECT carries `WHERE IS NOT NULL`. The reasoning is that the bridge's grain is one row per measurement event, and an event that did not occur is not a measurement event: emitting a row for an unshipped order and setting `shipped_orders_count = 1` on it makes "shipped orders" count orders that never shipped. The two alternatives were weighed honestly. A sentinel calendar member (the Kimball unknown-date trick) preserves `count(*)` per stage and makes "unshipped" a filter, but it stops the calendar being a calendar and puts a non-date in every time series. Coalescing to the entity's primary date fabricates a shipment in a month where none happened. The cost is specific and someone will trip over it: **"orders not yet shipped" is not a row count anywhere.** It is `sum(placed) − sum(shipped)` over the same period, or a separately declared measure on the placed stage. That is the same shape as conventions.md §2's rule that ratios are not stored — store the additive parts, combine at query time — so it is at least a familiar discipline rather than a new one. ## Measures, and why the event is the qualifier `dab/uss.yaml` measures are either `count` (the generator emits `cast(1 AS BIGINT)`) or `sum` of one named DAB attribute. **There is no free-text SQL in uss.yaml and no filter clause.** This is the rule that keeps first-time business logic out of DAR, and it has a consequence that turns out to be the deepest thing in the design: a measure that "needs a WHERE" is a different *event*. "Shipped orders" is not "placed orders with a filter"; it is the shipped stage. The event is the qualifier. That is why the bridge is event-based, and it connects straight back to `anatomy-of-business-question`'s anatomy — measure, dimensions, time grain — where the measure and its qualifier are one thing, not a metric plus an ad-hoc predicate. Every measure is additive at the bridge grain, so `sum()` is always the correct aggregate and `count(*)` is never a measure. `count(*)` over the bridge counts events of every kind mixed together and is meaningless — a permanent hazard, mitigated by the contract publishing which stage owns what, not removed by it. ## Files, and whether generated SQL is committed Generated SQL is **committed**, and CI regenerates and fails on any diff. This looks like it contradicts R4 ("Nothing here is hand-written or hand-edited") and in fact enforces it: the drift check turns "nobody edits generated output" from an aspiration into a failing test. The blog-synthesis lists "whether generated SQL is a reviewed surface" as unresolved in the corpus, so this is decided here rather than inherited. The affirmative argument is that the diff of the generated SQL *is* the review surface for a model change — the blueprint's own warning is that "Generation guarantees consistency, not correctness", and the diff is the only place a human sees what a one-line YAML change did to the layer every page reads. conventions.md §3 pushes the same way ("SQL that lives in a Python string is written to a file so the same linter sees it"). The cost is diff noise: a small model change can rewrite `_bridge.sql` wholesale, and reviewers learn to skim it, which is exactly how the review surface stops working. Generation runs `sqlfluff fix` as a post-step rather than teaching the generator about line layout — spike 4's recommendation, and it means the committed file and the regenerated file are byte-identical by construction. ## On conventions.md §1.3 Obeyed as written: `_measure____`, `
data.concreteShape:
## Files the generator emits (all committed under `dar/uss/`)

```
dar/uss/_bridge.sql        CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dar__uss._bridge      (UNION ALL of stages)
dar/uss/_calendar.sql      CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dar__uss._calendar
dar/uss/order.sql          CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dar__uss."order"      (one per entity)
dar/uss/checks.sql         one statement per invariant, each returning a violation count
dar/uss/sliceability.yaml  measure x key coverage contract (the pre-trust coverage report)
dar/uss/plan.yaml          objects in build order: peripherals -> _bridge -> _calendar
```

CLI: `uv run adss dar generate` (YAML -> files, no database, offline) · `uv run adss dar generate --check` (CI: regenerate, fail on any diff) · `uv run adss dar build` (execute `plan.yaml`) · `uv run adss dar check` (run `checks.sql`, every count must be 0).

## Input: `dab/uss.yaml` (slice 1)

```yaml
uss:
  events:
    - id: PLACED
      entity: ORDER
      definition: An order was placed, on the date the business records as its order date.
      date_attribute: PLACED_ON
      measures:
        - id: PLACED_ORDERS_COUNT
          definition: The number of orders placed, one per order, counted on the date it was placed.
          aggregate: count
  states: []
  exclude_relationships: []
```

`aggregate` is `count` (emits `cast(1 AS BIGINT)`) or `sum` with `attribute: <DAB_ATTRIBUTE>`. No SQL, no filters. Peripherals are derived from `model.yaml`, never declared.

## `dar__uss._bridge` — the complete column contract

| Column | Type | Null | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `_stage` | VARCHAR | no | the entity this row is a row *of*; equals the name of the peripheral whose key is guaranteed non-null here (`order`) |
| `_event` | VARCHAR | no | the event identifier, lower-cased (`placed`, `shipped`, `observed`) |
| `_event_date` | DATE | no | the date of the measurement event; joins `_calendar.date_key` |
| `_is_current` | BOOLEAN | no | TRUE if this row reflects the entity version currently in effect; always TRUE on a transaction stage |
| `_observed_at` | TIMESTAMP | no | DAB `eff_tmstp` of the version behind this row = DAS `extracted_at`; per-row provenance |
| `<entity>_key` | VARCHAR | own key: no; inherited: yes | one column per entity populated by at least one stage. Own key non-null; parent keys inherited along many-to-one edges; child keys never present |
| `_measure__<entity>__<measure>` | BIGINT for `count`, DECIMAL(28,8) for `sum` of a numeric attribute | non-null only on the owning stage | one column per declared measure. Non-owning branches emit `cast(NULL AS <T>)` |

Slice 1 instantiates: `_stage, _event, _event_date, _is_current, _observed_at, order_key, _measure__order__placed_orders_count`.

Rules the contract carries: every measure is additive at this grain, so `sum()` is always right and `count(*)` is never a measure. A join on the row's own `_stage` key may be INNER; a join on an inherited key must be LEFT. The column list grows additively with questions and is never narrowed.

## `dar__uss."order"` — peripheral (one per entity)

| Column | Type | Null | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `order_key` | VARCHAR | no | unique; the DAB business key value (`10248`) |
| `_observed_at` | TIMESTAMP | no | `eff_tmstp` of the current version |
| `order_id`, `order_status`, `order_ship_country`, … | VARCHAR / TIMESTAMP / DECIMAL(28,8) | yes | one per declared attribute, lower-cased attribute id unchanged |

Current-state, exactly one row per key. No `_is_current` (it could never vary). No `_stage`.

## `dar__uss._calendar` — the complete column contract

| Column | Type | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `date_key` | DATE | `1996-07-04` |
| `year_number` | INTEGER | `1996` |
| `quarter_of_year` | INTEGER | `3` |
| `month_of_year` | INTEGER | `7` |
| `day_of_month` | INTEGER | `4` |
| `year_start` | DATE | `1996-01-01` |
| `quarter_start` | DATE | `1996-07-01` |
| `month_start` | DATE | `1996-07-01` |
| `quarter_label` | VARCHAR | `1996-Q3` |
| `month_label` | VARCHAR | `1996-07` |

Dense daily rows from `min(_event_date)` to `max(_event_date)` over the whole bridge — a calendar containing only dates that occurred is not a calendar, and a month with no orders must still appear in a time series. Civil arithmetic only: no fiscal periods, no holidays, no ISO weeks. Those are business meaning and belong in DAB (blueprint B8), not invented by a generator.

## Worked example — the single transaction stage, house style

`dar/uss/_bridge.sql` (verified: executes on duckdb 1.5.5, lints clean under the repo's `.sqlfluff`)

```sql
-- Generated by `uv run adss dar generate`. Do not edit; edit dab/uss.yaml and regenerate.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dar__uss._bridge AS
WITH order_placed AS (
    SELECT
        o."ORDER_key" AS order_key,
        o.eff_tmstp AS observed_at,
        cast(o."PLACED_ON" AS DATE) AS event_date
    FROM dab."view_ORDER_hist" AS o
    WHERE o."PLACED_ON" IS NOT NULL
    QUALIFY row_number() OVER (
        PARTITION BY o."ORDER_key"
        ORDER BY o.eff_tmstp DESC
    ) = 1
)

SELECT
    'order' AS _stage,
    'placed' AS _event,
    op.event_date AS _event_date,
    TRUE AS _is_current,
    op.observed_at AS _observed_at,
    op.order_key AS order_key,
    cast(1 AS BIGINT) AS _measure__order__placed_orders_count
FROM order_placed AS op;
```

A second stage is a second CTE plus a `UNION ALL` branch that emits `cast(NULL AS BIGINT) AS _measure__order__placed_orders_count` and `cast(1 AS BIGINT) AS _measure__order__shipped_orders_count`. Verified end to end on three synthetic hist rows: placed total 2, shipped total 1, `count(*)` 3, ownership violations 0 — the unshipped order correctly has no shipment row.

Note the shape: `WHERE` before `QUALIFY` means the version collapse picks the latest version *in which the event is dated*. Mixed-case DAB identifiers are double-quoted (`"ORDER_key"`, `"PLACED_ON"`); lower-case framework columns (`eff_tmstp`) are not, because §3's quoting rule exists to make a mixed-case identifier's quotes visible. `QUALIFY` is why `.sqlfluff` must use the duckdb dialect.

## `dar/uss/_calendar.sql`

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dar__uss._calendar AS
WITH bounds AS (
    SELECT
        min(b._event_date) AS first_date,
        max(b._event_date) AS last_date
    FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b
),

calendar_day AS (
    SELECT
        cast(d.day_ts AS DATE) AS date_key
    FROM bounds AS bo,
        range(bo.first_date, bo.last_date + INTERVAL 1 DAY, INTERVAL 1 DAY) AS d (day_ts)
)

SELECT
    cd.date_key AS date_key,
    cast(year(cd.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS year_number,
    cast(quarter(cd.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS quarter_of_year,
    cast(month(cd.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS month_of_year,
    cast(day(cd.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS day_of_month,
    cast(date_trunc('year', cd.date_key) AS DATE) AS year_start,
    cast(date_trunc('quarter', cd.date_key) AS DATE) AS quarter_start,
    cast(date_trunc('month', cd.date_key) AS DATE) AS month_start,
    strftime(cd.date_key, '%Y') || '-Q' || cast(quarter(cd.date_key) AS VARCHAR) AS quarter_label,
    strftime(cd.date_key, '%Y-%m') AS month_label
FROM calendar_day AS cd;
```

## The slice-1 question against the contract

```sql
SELECT
    c.month_start AS month_start,
    o.order_ship_country AS order_ship_country,
    sum(b._measure__order__placed_orders_count) AS placed_orders_count
FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b
INNER JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS c ON b._event_date = c.date_key
INNER JOIN dar__uss."order" AS o ON b.order_key = o.order_key
WHERE b._event = 'placed'
GROUP BY c.month_start, o.order_ship_country
ORDER BY c.month_start, o.order_ship_country;
```

Lints clean. The marimo page casts the aggregate to DOUBLE before charting — spike 3 observed that DuckDB DECIMAL reaches polars as `decimal[38,0]` and altair cannot encode it; the cast belongs in the page, not in the bridge, so the bridge keeps DAB's precision.

Four checks, in the order they fail.

**1. Generator unit tests, test-first, against a neutral fixture model** (`tests/test_dar_generate.py`). Given a fixture model with entities `A` and `B` and a many-to-one edge `A -> B`, and a uss.yaml declaring one event and one count measure on `A`, the generator emits a `_bridge.sql` whose SELECT list is exactly `_stage, _event, _event_date, _is_current, _observed_at, a_key, b_key, _measure__a__…`, with `b_key` sourced from `view_A_<REL>_B` by LEFT JOIN and no `a_key` column on any `B`-rooted stage. Golden-file comparison on the emitted text. No entity, attribute or business term from the real model appears anywhere in `src/` or in this test — conventions §5 — which is what proves the generator is generic rather than asserting it.

**2. `uv run adss dar generate --check` in CI.** Regenerates every file (including the `sqlfluff fix` post-step) and fails if the working tree differs by one byte. This is blueprint R4 enforced mechanically: an edit to generated SQL is a build failure, not a convention.

**3. `uv run adss dar check` against the built warehouse** — generated invariants in `dar/uss/checks.sql`, each returning a violation count, all of which must be 0. The test that runs them iterates over the file and therefore also contains no data vocabulary:

- *Ownership (proves measures do not propagate):* `SELECT count(*) FROM dar__uss._bridge WHERE _measure__order__placed_orders_count IS NOT NULL AND NOT (_stage = 'order' AND _event = 'placed')` — one per measure.
- *Grain (proves nothing fanned inside a stage):* rows where `_stage='order' AND _event='placed'` equals `count(*)` over `dab."view_ORDER_hist"` after `WHERE "PLACED_ON" IS NOT NULL` and the same QUALIFY.
- *Peripheral uniqueness (proves the consumer's join is safe):* `count(*) = count(DISTINCT order_key)` on every peripheral, and `count(*)` of `_bridge LEFT JOIN "order" USING (order_key)` equals `count(*)` of `_bridge`.
- *Cardinality guard (proves the n:1 assumption, per walked edge):* `count(*) = count(DISTINCT <source>_key)` in `view_<S>_<REL>_<T>`. Failure stops the build; the only escape is an `exclude_relationships` entry naming the edge and the reason.
- *Calendar coverage:* no `_event_date` without a matching `_calendar.date_key`, and `count(*) = date_diff('day', min(date_key), max(date_key)) + 1` (density).
- *Sliceability agreement:* every (measure, key) pair marked sliceable in `sliceability.yaml` has at least one bridge row where both are non-null, and every pair marked not-sliceable has none.

**4. The question, computed twice, agrees.** `docs/questions/0001-*.md` holds both statements: the `das__staged` one (dedupe to the latest `extracted_at` per order id, `date_trunc('month', order_date)`, `count(*)`) and the `dar__uss` one above. CI asserts row-for-row equality. This is also the staleness detector: a DAB execute without a DAR rebuild makes them disagree.

The decision is still holding when all four are green *and* `sliceability.yaml`'s not-sliceable list is non-empty — an empty one means the walk stopped distinguishing directions.

consequences.text: Additivity stops being a discipline and becomes a build-time property that a generated check asserts. The ownership invariant (`a measure column is non-null only on its owning stage`) is one line of SQL per measure and it fails the moment anyone copies a parent measure down a relationship, which is the single most common way a consumption layer starts double-counting.

Every process lands on one dense calendar, so a question spanning placement and shipment is one GROUP BY rather than a union of two stars. This is the thing the event grain buys, and it is the reason the shared-structure deviation D-0001 is worth its price.

The next question costs a marimo page, not a model. Adding an entity, an event or a measure is a new stage or a new column — additive in DAR the way blueprint B7 is additive in DAB — and every existing page keeps working because nothing it names changes.

Coverage is inspectable before anyone trusts it. `sliceability.yaml` is derived mechanically from the same walk that builds the bridge, so `can I break this measure down by that key` is a lookup, and the absences (orders by product, for instance) are published rather than discovered by getting a wrong number.

Reading only `view_<E>_hist` and `view_<S>_<REL>_<T>` keeps DAR off daana's physical internals — `_desc`, `_x`, `_idfr`, `_focal`, the DuckDB table macros — which 0.7.0 has already demonstrated it is willing to change underneath downstream consumers.

The generator is a pure function of two YAML files, so it unit-tests against a neutral fixture model with no warehouse and no data vocabulary in `src/` or in tests, which is what conventions §5 asks for and what proves the machinery is source-agnostic rather than asserting it.

The column contract is a public API with no deprecation path. Every page names `_measure__order__placed_orders_count` and `order_key` literally. Renaming a measure in `dab/uss.yaml` renames a column and breaks every consumer at once; there is no aliasing view layer and no per-reader projection (that is exactly what D-0001 gave up). The first measure rename is the day this cost is paid, and it will be paid in full.

`count(*)` on the bridge is meaningless and it is the most natural thing an analyst will type. The bridge mixes events of different kinds on different dates, so its row count is neither the number of orders nor the number of shipments — the two-stage worked example gives 2 placed, 1 shipped, and `count(*)` = 3. The sliceability contract mitigates this; it does not remove it, and no amount of documentation will stop it happening in a PivotTable.

An entity whose event date is null produces no row, so `orders not yet shipped` is not a row count anywhere in the system. It is `sum(placed) - sum(shipped)` over a period, or a separately declared measure. Somebody will count rows in the shipped stage, subtract from an order total taken at a different grain, and be wrong in a way that looks arithmetically fine.

Full rebuild only. The blog's incremental recipe (`WHERE ver_tmstp > last_run_tmstp`, plus a persisted watermark) is not implementable on the view contract spike 2 observed: `ver_tmstp` appears on `view_<S>_<REL>_<T>` and on neither `view_<E>` nor `view_<E>_hist`. At Northwind scale this is free; it is a wall at any real volume, and the fix requires either a daana change or reading `_desc` directly, which this record forbids.

Materialising DAR does not decouple readers from the DAB rebuild, because it is one DuckDB file. Spike 2 observed that any other open connection — including a read-only one — makes `daana-cli execute` fail with the actively misleading error `daana framework is not installed on the remote database`. The marimo page must be stopped for every build, and whoever operates it has to be told that this error means the file is busy.

Peripheral attributes are current-state, so joining them gives today's values to a historical bridge row. Slice 1's answer per ship country will move retroactively if a source restates ShipCountry, and `as it was recorded then` is not answerable until a state stage exists. This is a Type-1 dimension by construction, chosen deliberately, and it is the kind of thing that is discovered during an audit rather than during development.

A many-to-many relationship added in DAB stops DAR generation. daana 0.7.0 supports M:N first-class; the cardinality guard fails the build and the only escape is an explicit `exclude_relationships` entry. That is the right failure — silent fan-out is worse — but it means a DAB modeller can block the DAR build with a change that is perfectly valid in their own layer.

Committing generated SQL means a one-line YAML change can rewrite `_bridge.sql` wholesale. The diff is meant to be the review surface for model changes; a diff that is large and mechanical every time is a diff reviewers learn to skim, which is precisely how a review surface stops working.

The bridge is wide and sparse by construction: with k entities and m measures every stage emits mostly NULLs. Harmless at this scale, and the largest object in the file at any other. The wide-table cost the blueprint warns about in DAB reappears here — deliberately, because DAR is allowed to be shaped for consumption, but it is still real.

data.contextAndProblem:
DAR is the layer every consumer is written against, and this record fixes the column names those consumers will type. `_measure__order__placed_orders_count` is not an implementation detail; it is the string in the marimo page, in the second page, and in whatever reads this warehouse in year three. Blueprint R4 makes the layer regenerable but gives no deprecation path: regeneration under a changed contract does not migrate a consumer, it breaks one. So the cost of getting this wrong is not rework in DAR, it is rework in everything downstream of DAR, forever, and slice 1 exercises almost none of it — one entity, one event, one count, no relationships. Nearly every column being fixed here will be unexercised and permanent on the day it lands.

The obvious answer — "generate the Unified Star Schema the blog describes" — is not available as written, because the blog contradicts itself on the one point that matters most. `consumption-layer-generates-itself` says the walk follows many-to-one edges and inherits "the keys **and measures** of everything you reach". The diagram directly beneath that sentence shows three order lines rolling up to one order: the safe n:1 walk gives `sum(order.revenue) = 100`, "counted once", while pushing the order's 100 down onto each of its three lines gives 300, "fan-out, ×3". But copying a parent's measure onto every child row *is* the second picture. If measures propagated the way the sentence says, the safe walk would produce the unsafe number. The post's own worked example refutes its own rule, and no reading of the post resolves it. That has to be resolved here, precisely, because "inherit everything along it" implemented literally is a silent doubling.

The second difficulty is that daana's published interface does not contain the things a USS generator naturally reaches for, and spike 2 established this by observation rather than inference. `view_<entity>_with_rel` — the object whose name promises denormalised foreign keys — carries none: its column list is byte-identical to `view_<entity>`, with no `CUSTOMER_key` on `view_ORDER_with_rel`. `<entity>_focal` and `<entity>_idfr` are created and never populated on DuckDB (0 rows each, while `CUSTOMER_desc` holds 25 and the views still return correct results), so a generator designed against the PostgreSQL run joins them and silently returns nothing. And `model.yaml` declares relationships with only `source_entity_id`, `target_entity_id`, `name` and `definition` — **no cardinality at all** — while the entire many-to-one walk is a function of cardinality. The one input the generator most needs does not exist in the model it must read.

The third difficulty is what "history" means in this system, and it is not what the USS literature assumes. By the prior decision, DAB history is dated by `extracted_at` — `eff_tmstp` is `to_timestamp(cast(_dlt_load_id AS DOUBLE))`. So the `view_<E>_hist` timeline is an **observation** timeline: when we saw a value, not when it was true. Business validity intervals do not exist in this warehouse unless a business date attribute carries them. That means a question about something that *happened* and a question about a state *as observed* are dated by two entirely different clocks, and a bridge that conflates them will answer "how many orders were placed in July 1996" with a number that moves whenever we reload.

Fourth, the corpus does not agree that a USS is even the right shape. `why-we-built-daana` says "dimensional modeling remains the natural choice for the DAR layer"; `ai-assisted-data-engineering` describes an agent building Kimball facts, dimensions and snapshots with conformed dimensions; `consumption-layer-generates-itself` says stop sorting tables into facts and dimensions altogether. The blog-synthesis names this "the single biggest unresolved conflict" in eighteen posts. And even within the USS post, the build target is written `order_line.bridge` (per entity) while the sample SQL queries a single `_bridge`, with no explanation of the relationship — and that sample SQL selects `t.territory_key` with no `t` anywhere in its `FROM`.

Finally, the escape hatches are already spent. Deviation D-0001 is registered and open: there is one shared `dar__uss`, no per-consumer projection, and its own cost entry says "there is no per-reader projection, so 'this reader may not see freight' cannot be expressed" and "two readers cannot hold different definitions of the same measure". Whatever contract this record fixes is the contract for every consumer simultaneously, with no room to differ.
decisionDrivers: Additivity must be a property of the build, not a discipline the analyst remembers: 'Not additive if you remember to be careful. Additive by construction' [consumption-layer-generates-itself]
The generated column names are a public API with no deprecation path — D-0001 removed the per-reader projection that could have absorbed a rename
The generator must be a pure function of the YAML model, so it is testable offline against a neutral fixture with no data vocabulary in src/ or tests (conventions §5)
DAR may read only DAB, and only DAB's published view interface — not its physical `_desc`/`_x`/`_idfr`/`_focal` tables, which 0.7.0 has already changed under downstream consumers once
Every question must be computable twice — from das__staged and from dar__uss — and agree, so the contract must be stable enough to write both statements against
A wrong answer must fail loudly rather than look plausible: a missing column beats an all-NULL one, a failed build beats a warning in a log
Nothing in DAR is hand-edited (blueprint R4), which has to be enforced by a check rather than by convention
Slice 1 fixes columns it does not exercise, so the contract must be right for the state stage, the second entity and the second event before any of them exist
Business meaning is defined exactly once, in DAB (blueprint B8) — so the generator may do civil-calendar arithmetic but must not invent a fiscal year, and uss.yaml may not contain SQL
consideredOptions: Generated event-grained Puppini bridge: one `_bridge` unioning per-(entity, event) stages that own their measures and inherit only keys along many-to-one paths, plus one current-state peripheral per entity and one dense calendar
Puppini-canonical bridge: `_bridge` carries the stage column and the keys only, with all measures left on the peripheral tables where the entity's own attributes live
Entity-grained bridge: one row per entity instance carrying several date columns (placed_on, shipped_on, required_on) instead of one row per measurement event
Generated Kimball star per business process: a fact table per process, dimension tables, and one shared date dimension
Generated One Big Table per question: flatten the entity, its parents' attributes and its measures into a single wide table per business question
No generator: one hand-written view or query per business question, reviewed like any other SQL
groundedIn: consumption-layer-generates-itself: 'Instead of one row per entity instance, you make the bridge event-based: one row per measurement event, each carrying its own date... One calendar, every process.' — this is what forces event grain and the single calendar
consumption-layer-generates-itself: 'The rule is short: follow any path that never fans out, and inherit everything along it.' — the sentence that, read literally, would multiply measures

consumption-layer-generates-itself, the revenue panel, verbatim: 'walk n:1 · lines → order ... sum(order.revenue) 100 ✓ counted once' vs 'walk 1:n · order → lines ... sum(revenue) 300 ✗ fan-out, ×3' — the diagram that contradicts the sentence and settles the reading
consumption-layer-generates-itself: 'A many-to-many step has no safe direction at all, so the generator skips it and tells you.' — becomes the cardinality guard plus an explicit exclude entry

consumption-layer-generates-itself, sliceability panel, verbatim: 'SELECT t.territory_key, SUM(b._measure__order_line__revenue) FROM _bridge b GROUP BY 1' — fixes `_measure__<entity>__<measure>` and `<entity>_key`, and shows a `t.` alias with no `t` in FROM, which is why the keys must be on the bridge
consumption-layer-generates-itself: 'USS = bridge + peripherals' (projections diagram) — 'peripherals' is named twice and never defined anywhere in the post
consumption-layer-generates-itself: 'a single bridge is a PivotTable's best friend' — the bridge must be a single physically-consumable wide table, not only a semantic surface

design-of-analytical-systems: 'reuse the definition, never reuse the instance' and 'Star Schema... This is where Star Schema belongs' — DAR may hold a star; it may not hold shared structure without cost, which D-0001 already prices

daana-cli-0-7-0-release: 'view_<entity>_hist returns one row per value-run... Audit consumers that need every observation should query <entity>_desc directly.' — DAR reads _hist; we do not ask 'how many times was this loaded'

daana-cli-0-7-0-release: 'Cluster keys restructured to favor ver_tmstp (system load time) over eff_tmstp... enables incremental DAR builds via the WHERE ver_tmstp > last_run_tmstp pattern' — the recipe we cannot use, because ver_tmstp is not on the entity views

integration-by-design-analytical-identifiers, via synthesis: 'DAR joins only on {ENTITY}_key; the _idfr table is an integration mechanism, not a reporting dimension. Downstream tables see the result, not the resolution.'

anatomy-of-business-question: 'What is the [AGGREGATION] of [MEASURE] per [DIMENSION], [DIMENSION]?' and 'Is week ISO week or something else?' — why the event is the qualifier and why the calendar carries no week column until a question names one

Spike 2 observed (verbatim): 'DESCRIBE dab.view_ORDER_with_rel: ORDER_key VARCHAR | order_id VARCHAR | order_status VARCHAR | order_purchase_ts TIMESTAMP | order_value_amount DECIMAL(28,8) | order_value_currency VARCHAR [6 rows] ... (no CUSTOMER_key column; compare view_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER which does have ORDER_key + CUSTOMER_key)'

Spike 2 observed (verbatim): 'CUSTOMER_focal 0 / CUSTOMER_idfr 0 / CUSTOMER_desc 25 / ORDER_focal 0 / ORDER_idfr 0 / ORDER_desc 12 / ORDER_CUSTOMER_x 3 ... (yet SELECT * FROM dab.view_CUSTOMER returns the correct 3 rows with correct current values)' — _focal and _idfr are created but never populated on DuckDB

Spike 2 observed: 'DESCRIBE dab.view_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER: ORDER_key VARCHAR | CUSTOMER_key VARCHAR | type_key BIGINT | eff_tmstp TIMESTAMP | ver_tmstp TIMESTAMP', with 3 rows for 3 orders — the only source of relationship keys, and one row per source key

Spike 2 observed: 'DESCRIBE dab.view_customer: CUSTOMER_key VARCHAR | customer_id | ...' and 'DESCRIBE dab.view_customer_hist: CUSTOMER_key VARCHAR | eff_tmstp TIMESTAMP | ...' — the current view carries no eff_tmstp and neither entity view carries ver_tmstp

Spike 2 observed: with `entity_effective_timestamp_expression: das_load_ts`, 'eff_tmstp in view_<entity>_hist IS the DAS load timestamp verbatim' and 'view_CUSTOMER_hist' kept both the 2026-01-10 and 2026-02-15 versions of C001 — history is an observation timeline

Spike 2 observed: '<entity>_key is the natural business key value ('C001', 'O100'), not a surrogate' and 'Numeric attributes are widened to DECIMAL(28,8) regardless of the source column type' (source was DECIMAL(12,2))

Spike 2 observed: 'if any other process holds the .duckdb file open — read-write OR READ-ONLY — daana-cli execute fails, and the error it reports is completely wrong: daana framework is not installed on the remote database'

Spike 2 observed: object names preserve the model's casing on DuckDB ('view_CUSTOMER', 'CUSTOMER_focal'), so 'code that string-matches names out of information_schema WILL break' — the generator renders names from the model instead

Spike 4 observed: on generated SQL with 'UNION ALL of 3 branches, every column AS-aliased, cast(x AS DECIMAL(28,8)) ... QUALIFY row_number() OVER (...), quoted reserved word dab."order"' only RF06 fires — and AL09/RF06/LT05/LT09 'structurally contradict how a code generator emits SQL and must be excluded'

Spike 4 observed: 'RF02 ... is the one rule sqlfluff CANNOT auto-fix' and 'LT14 ... FIX THE GENERATOR, but for free — sqlfluff fix repairs it automatically. Just run sqlfluff fix as a generation post-step'

Spike 3 observed: 'DuckDB DECIMAL columns arrive as polars decimal[38,0] and altair cannot encode them. CAST aggregates to DOUBLE in the SQL (this is a DAR-view design decision, not a notebook workaround)'

Verified here on duckdb 1.5.5: the worked bridge SQL collapses two versions of order 10248 to the 2026-09-05 one and drops no orders; the two-stage union yields placed total 2, shipped total 1, count(*) 3, ownership violations 0, with the unshipped order emitting no shipment row

Verified here on sqlfluff 4.3.0 with the repo's own .sqlfluff: the bridge, calendar, peripheral and consumer queries all lint clean — but RF04 ('Keywords should not be used as identifiers') fires on calendar columns named year, quarter, month and day, which is why they are year_number, quarter_of_year, month_of_year and day_of_month

daana-cli --help (the only thing read from that repository): the commands are check, deploy, execute, generate, init, install, lint, merge, ui — there is no DAR or USS generation command, so the generator is ours to build
blueprint.md R4: 'Volatile and generated. Nothing here is hand-written or hand-edited... An edit to generated output is lost on the next generation'; B8: 'Meaning is defined exactly once, here'

conventions.md §1.3: '_bridge, _calendar, _stage, _event, _event_date, _is_current, _measure__…' and 'Measure columns are _measure__<entity>__<measure>' — the contract this record completes; and §3: 'No SELECT * ... except a union of stages whose column list the generator fixes'

deviations.md D-0001 (open): 'keys inherit along many-to-one relationships, measures stay on the stage that owns them' — the register already states the rule this record has to implement, and prices its cost
notSettled: Relationship cardinality is declared nowhere. daana's model.yaml carries only source_entity_id, target_entity_id, name and definition, and daana-cli 0.7.0 added first-class M:N support — so the n:1 assumption rests on conventions §1.2's verb-phrase direction rule plus one spike observation of 3 rows for 3 orders. The build-time guard makes it falsifiable, but whether it should instead be declared in dab/uss.yaml (at the cost of a second home for a modelling fact) is a live question the first M:N relationship will reopen.

Whether `<entity>_focal` and `<entity>_idfr` are populated on PostgreSQL. Spike 2 saw both empty on DuckDB and flagged this as untested elsewhere. It does not change what the generator reads, but it decides whether this is a DuckDB defect worth reporting or a vestigial pair of tables.

What FULL and FULL_LOG do to a key that disappears from the source. Spike 2 ran out of time-box: '_desc has row_st, sta_tmstp and end_tmstp columns that are all currently Y/NULL/NULL, so the machinery for it exists — but I did not exercise it.' If a deleted order stops appearing in view_<E>_hist, bridge history changes retroactively and blueprint B3's reproducibility claim is not true.

Whether `view_<S>_<REL>_<T>` is one row per source key under every ingestion strategy. Observed under TRANSACTIONAL only; 0.7.0's 'active member set' semantics for `_has_` views suggest the relationship view may be set-shaped for M:N, which would fan the key join.

Incremental build. The blog's recipe is `WHERE ver_tmstp > last_run_tmstp` with a persisted watermark, but ver_tmstp appears only on the relationship view, not on view_<E> or view_<E>_hist. Full rebuild is the only implementable option on the observed contract; whether to add a watermark table now, or wait for a daana change, is undecided.

The serialization standard for the sliceability contract. The post says 'a vendor-neutral semantic contract (e.g. OSI)' and exemplifies rather than fixes it. This record emits a bespoke sliceability.yaml; whether that becomes OSI, MetricFlow or an MCP tool surface is deferred to whoever needs a second consumer.

Whether the bridge should carry an `_event_ts TIMESTAMP` alongside `_event_date`. No question has asked for intraday grain, and the contract grows additively, so it is omitted — but the day one arrives, whether to add the column or a second calendar is an open choice.

Whether conventions §1.2's entity-prefix guideline should be dropped for attributes that will only ever live on their own peripheral. Keeping it gives `order.order_ship_country`; dropping it gives `order.ship_country` and pushes the disambiguation into the OBT projection. It is a Guideline, so either is legal, and the implementer decides per attribute.

Whether a state stage should be added in slice 1 at all, or whether `_is_current` should stay constant TRUE until a question needs history. The column contract admits both; the record fixes the shape without instantiating it.

Whether the double computation is a real check or a tautology in the part that matters. Both statements express the same version-collapse rule (QUALIFY on the latest extraction), written twice. It genuinely validates the DAB mapping and the walk against parquet DAB never touched; it does not independently validate the collapse rule itself.

How a business calendar (fiscal periods, holidays) enters the system. This record forbids the generator from inventing one — that is business meaning and B8 puts it in DAB — but whether DAB models a CALENDAR_DAY entity that the walk reaches, or the calendar gains a declared mapping, is unresolved and the first fiscal-quarter request will force it.

Whether measures declared in dab/uss.yaml stay reusable. B6 forbids anything in DAB existing because one consumer wanted it; a measure declared for a page is exactly that. The rule here is that uss.yaml declares business measures and events and nothing page-specific, but there is no check that enforces it, and a per-page section appearing in uss.yaml is the observable sign B6 has broken.
data.recommendation: Generated event-grained Puppini bridge: one `_bridge` unioning per-(entity, event) stages that own their measures and inherit only keys along many-to-one paths, plus one current-state peripheral per entity and one dense calendar
data.title: DAR is one generated Unified Star Schema: an event-grained bridge whose stages own their measures and inherit only keys, one current-state peripheral per entity, one dense calendar, and a column contract fixed before the first page is written
